entries.title: Amos 1:1 "Amos"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:1 "Amos" For the supposed meanings of this rare name see Introduction, I., B.

▣ "the sheepherders" This term occurs only one other time in the OT, "sheepmaster," used of Mesha, King of Moab (cf. 2 Kgs. 3:4). Amos' occupation could also relate to the care of cattle (BDB 133, cf. Amos 7:14). This is an unusual term (BDB 667, KB 719-720) and could refer to the ownership of a special kind of diminutive sheep (BDB 838, cf. Amos 7:15). Amos was

  1. following Jewish tradition, a well-to-do businessman (sheep breeder, cf. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1177)
  2. he was a poor herdsman and itinerant agricultural worker

The Hebrew consonantal root נקד (KB 719-720) has many meanings.

  1. to prick, to puncture
  2. to clean, to shine (Arabic, "to free" or "to save")
  3. a poor type of sheep
  4. money (Talmud, a small coin)
  5. speckled (cf. Gen. 30:32)
  6. shepherd, herdsman, sheep breeder
  7. title for high official (Ugaritic)

Context is crucial! Only context defines words. Cognates are only helpful when the word is rare. In Amos there are several words used to describe his occupation before his call by God.

  1. "shepherd," Amos 1:1 (BDB 667)
  2. "herdsman," Amos 7:14 (BDB 133)
  3. "from following the flock," Amos 7:15 (BDB 29 CONSTRUCT BDB 838)

▣ "Tekoa" The name (BDB 1075, KB 1785) means "to pitch a tent" (cf. Gen. 31:25; Jer: 6:3) or "to blow a trumpet" (cf. Ezek. 7:14). Tekoa is a city in the Judean desert, overlooking the Judean wilderness. It was about five miles south of Bethlehem. Isn't it amazing how many of God's leaders have come from the pastoral lifestyle?

▣ "which he envisioned in visions" The term is literally "saw" (BDB 302, KB 301, Qal PERFECT). It is regularly used of an ecstatic vision (cf. Num. 24:4,16; Isa. 1:1; 2:1,13; Ezek. 12:27; 13:16; Micah 1:1; Hab. 1:1). It came to be one of three words used to designate a prophet (i.e. "seer," e.g. Amos 7:12; 2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Kgs. 17:13; 1 Chr. 21:9; 29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29; 12:15; 19:2; 29:25,29; 33:19; 35:15; Isa. 29:10,25; 30:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHET (the different Hebrew terms)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "the days of Uzziah king of Judah" He was a godly king who reigned in Judah from 783-742 B.C. The fact that the king of Judah was mentioned at all shows the prophet's theological orientation toward Jerusalem. The prophets always condemn the splitting of the tribes in 922 B.C. (cf. 1 Kgs. 12:16-20; 2 Chronicles 10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "the days of Jeroboam. . .king of Israel" This refers to Jeroboam II (BDB 914), who reigned over the Northern Ten Tribes from 786-746 B.C. He was a very successful and efficient Monarch. Both Judah and Israel, at this period, were enjoying great prosperity because Assyria had defeated their traditional enemy to the north, Syria. Also, Assyria and Egypt were not expansionists during this period (see Introduction, VI).

▣ "two years before the earthquake" This must have been a very strong earthquake because it is mentioned years later in Zech. 14:5. It may be alluded to in Amos 8:8 and 9:1. Josephus (Antiq. 9.225) tells us that it is related to Uzziah's sin of offering of a sacrifice (cf. 2 Chr. 26:16-21). This is either

  1. a historical statement in an attempt to precisely set the date for Amos' prophecy (Amos 1:1 is the most extensive dating attempt of any book of the OT)
  2. a way of reinforcing the judgment theme of Amos' message from YHWH

See note in NET Bible, p. 1589, #6.

entries.title: Amos Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO AMOS

  1. NAME OF BOOK

    1. It is named after the prophet.

    2. The name "Amos" could mean:
      1. "to be a burden" (BDB 770, KB 846)
      2. "to carry a burden" (BDB 770, KB 846)
      3. "to sustain" (possibly "YHWH has carried" [KB 847]. It may be a shortened form of Amasiah, which means "YHWH hears," cf. 2 Chr. 17:16).
      4. One rabbinical tradition asserts that it was a title given to him by those who opposed his message, implying he did not speak clearly or he stuttered.

    3. This is the only occurrence of this name in the Old Testament. Isaiah's father, "Amoz" (cf. Isa. 1:1) is spelled differently. There is an Amos mentioned in the genealogy of Luke 3:25, but nothing is known of him.

  2. CANONIZATION

    1. This book is part of the division of the Hebrew canon called "the latter prophets."
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON

    2. It is one of "the Twelve" Minor Prophets (i.e. shorter prophetic books, all contained on one scroll).

    3. The order of "the Twelve" or Minor Prophets has been linked by many scholars to a chronological sequence. However, there are problems with this view:
      1. The first six books are different between the MT and LXX
        MT LXX
        Hosea Hosea
        Joel Amos
        Amos Micah
        Obadiah Joel
        Jonah Obadiah
        Micah Jonah
      2. Internal evidence puts Amos chronologically before Hosea.
      3. The date for Joel is highly debated. I list him as an early post-exilic prophet along with Obadiah.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART

  3. GENRE

    1. This is the first of the writing prophets and sets the genre for all who follow.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

    2. This is classical Hebrew propheticism. This is a good example of Hebrew poetry and imagery.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

    3. Amos' writings or sayings, collected into a scroll, begin a wonderful literary form known as the "latter prophets" (Isaiah ‒ Malachi).
       Amos used the funeral dirge meter to emotionally communicate God's coming judgment. Form, meter, and content powerfully drive home the message of judgment.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, JUSTICE

    4. Here are some good quotes.
      1. A good summary of the prophets of this period is found in The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, "Amos."

        "At the same time, however, the eighth century witnessed the rise of one of the most potent moral forces the world has ever known—the writing prophets. These men, from widely separated backgrounds, shared an overwhelming conviction that God had called them. They had various styles of writing, but all wrote with the authority of the Almighty. They denounced the sins of their contemporaries and also looked far into the future as they spoke of deliverance for both Jew and Gentile" (p. 269).

      2. Kyle M. Yates, Studies in Amos.

        "Amos was a person who could never be taken for granted. Whether one agreed with his views or not, the impact of the prophet's message was lasting. The past twenty-seven centuries have not blunted this impact. Any person who looks deeply into the character of this man of God, and studies seriously the message of the prophet, will never be the same. He cannot accept casually the injustices of present-day society nor overlook God's concern for all of his children" (p. 1).

      3. Theo Laetsch, The Minor Prophets.

        "Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah, four great stars in the galaxy of Old Testament prophets, truly noble men of God, trying—alas, vainly—to stem the flood of iniquity engulfing God's people, and their inevitable ruin. Never has the holy Law of God been preached with greater earnestness and intensity than it was proclaimed by these men, who spared neither rich nor poor, neither young nor old, neither rebel nor hypocrite. And in no other period of the Old Testament era has the Gospel been heralded in language clearer and sweeter than these men spoke by inspiration of God. Yet all their faithful efforts, all their fervent appeals to their countrymen, could not hold back the overwhelming floodwaters of God's judgment sweeping away a people highly favored but unspeakably wicked and ungrateful. Still they continued in their call to repentance and salvation to a hardened generation, seeing but little success, yet faithful to their high calling. Their message is as timely today as it was more than 2,500 years ago. It is God's Word, enduring forever!" (p. 136)

  4. AUTHORSHIP

    1. Jewish tradition has always asserted the author to be Amos of Tekoa (cf. Amos 1:1).

    2. The man:
      1. He was a Judean from Tekoa (known for its "wise" people, cf. 2 Sam. 14), which is about five miles southeast of Bethlehem, located on the highest hill (2,700') in the region (cf. The International Standard Bible Encyclopaedia vol. 1, p. 120).
      2. He was not a prophet nor part of the prophetic family or guild (cf. Amos 7:14). Originally prophets lived together in communities. Later some became identified with the palace.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)
      3. He was apparently a "small sheep" (Arabic) herder (BDB 667, KB 719-720, cf. Amos 1:1, possibly
        1. "sheep herder"
        2. "sheep seller"
        3. "sheep owner" [cf. 2 Kgs. 3:4])
        4. A different and common term for "shepherd" (BDB 133) is used for him in Amos 7:14.
      4. He was (a) an owner of fruit trees or (b) a "dresser of sycamore trees" (cf. Amos 7:14). This may have involved an annual move to other locations. These trees are called "fig-mulberry." The fruit is much like a fig. Each fig had to be pierced individually by hand in order to ripen properly. This was a very important crop to the Near Eastern people. David even appointed a special supervisor (cf. 1 Chr. 27:28) to oversee these crops. Amos' agricultural background is the source of several of his prophecies.
        1. Amos 1:2
          (1) wild animals, Amos 3:3-8; 5:19
          (2) poor pasture land
          (3) drought
        2. Amos 2:13, weighted wagon
        3. Amos 4:6-9
          (1) lack of bread, Amos 4:6
          (2) no rain for crops, Amos 4:7
          (3) no water to drink, Amos 4:8
          (4) dry wind, Amos 4:9
          (5) mildew, Amos 4:9
          (6) insects, Amos 4:9
        4. Amos 5:16-17
          (1) mourning farmers, Amos 5:16
          (2) failing vineyards, Amos 5:17
        5. Amos 7:1-6
          (1) locusts, Amos 7:1-2
          (2) fire, Amos 7:4
        6. Amos 8:1-2, summer fruit
        7. Amos 9:13-15, days of agricultural prosperity, which denoted YHWH's presence and blessing (cf. Deut. 27-29).
      5. Jewish tradition says he was a well-to-do businessman. This is quite different from the common view today that he was a poor country peasant. Because of the excellency of his poetry and literary expertise the Jewish tradition is probably correct. From 2 Sam. 14:2ff we know that Tekoa was apparently known for its wise citizens. He was the first prophet to have his messages recorded in a separate scroll. Notice the FIRST PERSON, SINGULAR PRONOUNS in Amos 5:1; 7:1-9; 8:1, and 9:1.
      6. He preached to the northern kingdom of Israel. We know for certain that Bethel (i.e. site of Jeroboam II's golden calf) was a preaching site, but probably there were many other preaching locations.

    3. The issue of authorship is problematic because:
      1. The book implies he was a poor farm worker.
      2. The style and poetry are excellent, implying a well educated person.
      3. His sermons are said to have been given orally, but they are very structured and balanced, which implies written literature.
      4. Many scholars assume Amos had editorial or scribal help. One possible evidence of a scribe is that Amos 7:10-17 are in the THIRD PERSON, while Amos 7:1-9; 8:1-2; 9:1 are in the FIRST PERSON (cf. The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, p. 271).
      5. As with much of the OT, we moderns do not know how or when these biblical books were structured or formed. However, the ultimate author is the Spirit of God. It is their content that is crucial. They are a word from God to every age and culture, especially ones of prosperity and power!
        SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

  5. DATE

    1. It is relatively easy to date this prophecy about 750 B.C., plus or minus ten years.

    2. The first verse of Amos is the longest and most precise dating attempt of any OT book.
      1. Uzziah reigned from about 783-742 B.C. (Bright)
      2. Jeroboam II reigned from about 786-746 B.C. (Bright)
      3. The earthquake is also an attempt to date the book (cf. Amos 1:1; 8:8; 9:1,5; Zech. 14:5). Josephus related it to 2 Chr. 26:16-21 when Uzziah offered a sacrifice. Archaeological studies at Hazor suggest about 760 B.C. (Yadin, 1964).
        SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

    3. In Amos 5:8 and 8:9 an eclipse is mentioned. This may be the same one mentioned in Assyrian documents as occurring on June 15, 763 B.C. (Assyrian records), however, there was another complete eclipse on February 9, 784 B.C.

    4. Amos' encounter with Amaziah, the ruling priest at Bethel under the authority of Jeroboam II, also dates this book (cf. Amos 7:10-17).

  6. HISTORICAL SETTING

    1. The parallel biblical material is found in
      1. 2 Kgs. 14:3-17:6
      2. 2 Chr. 25-28
      3. Amos
      4. Jonah
      5. Hosea
      6. Isaiah
      7. Micah

    2. The simplest summary of the state of idolatry among God's people can be seen in Hosea.
      1. Hosea 2:16, "will no longer call me Baali"
      2. Hosea 4:12-13, ". . .daughters play the harlot. . ."
      3. Hosea 4:17, "Ephraim is joined to idols; Let him alone"
      4. Hosea 13:2, "men kiss calves!" (ritual)

    3. Social setting
      1. It was a time of economic prosperity and military expansion for both Israel and Judah. However, this prosperity was beneficial only to the wealthy class. The poor and middle classes were exploited and abused. It almost seems that "the buck and the gun" became additional idols!
      2. The social stability and property of both Israel and Judah are related to several causes:
        1. the long and prosperous reigns of Jeroboam II (786-746 B.C.) in the north and Uzziah (783-742 B.C.) in the south
        2. the temporary decline of Egypt and Mesopotamia
        3. Assyrians' defeat of Syria by Adad-Nirari III in 805 B.C.
        4. the lack of conflict between Israel and Judah
        5. the taxation and exploitation of the trade routes from north to south through the land bridge of Palestine caused rapid economic growth, even extravagance for the wealthy class
      3. The "Ostraca of Samaria," which are dated during the reign of Jeroboam II seem to indicate an administrative organization much like Solomon's. This seems to confirm the widening gap between the haves and have nots.
      4. The dishonesty of the wealthy is clearly depicted in Amos, who is called "the prophet of social justice." The bribery of the judiciary and the falsification of commercial weights are two clear examples of the abuse that was common, apparently in both Israel and Judah.

    4. Religious setting
      1. It was a time of much outward religious activity, but very little true faith. The fertility cults of Canaan had been amalgamated into Israel's religion. The people were idolaters, but they called it YHWHism. The trend of God's people toward political alliances had involved them in pagan worship and practices.
      2. The idolatry of Israel is spelled out in 2 Kgs. 17:7-18.
        1. v. 8, they followed the worship practices of the Canaanites
          (1) fertility worship
          (a) high places, 2 Kgs. 17:9,10.11
          (b) sacred pillars (Ba'al), 2 Kgs. 17:10,16
          (c) Asherim, 2 Kgs. 17:16, these were wooden symbols of the female consort of Ba'al. They were either curved stakes or live trees.
          (2) divination, 2 Kgs. 17:17, this is discussed in detail in Lev. 19-20 and Deut. 18.
        2. 2 Kgs. 17:16, they continued the worship of the two golden calves, symbolizing YHWH, set up at Dan and Bethel by Jeroboam I (1 Kgs. 12:28-29).
        3. 2 Kgs. 17:16, they worshiped the astral deities of Babylon: sun, moon, stars, and constellations.
        4. 2 Kgs. 17:18, they worshiped the Phoenician fertility fire god, Molech (cf. Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5).
      3. Ba'alism (cf. W. F. Albright's Archaeology and the Religion of Israel, p. 82ff).
        1. Our best source is "Ba'al Epic of Ugarit."
          (1) Depicts Ba'al as a seasonal dying and rising god. He was defeated by Mot and confined to the underworld. All life on earth ceased. But, helped by the female goddess, he rises and defeats Mot each spring. He is a fertility deity who was worshiped by imitation magic.
          (2) He was also known as Hadad (name of Syrian rulers). Many Syrian kings were called by this name.
        2. El is the chief deity of the Canaanite pantheon, but Ba'al's popularity usurped his place.
        3. Israel was most influenced by Tyrian Ba'alism through Jezebel, who was the daughter of the King of Tyre. She was chosen by Omri for his son Ahab.
        4. In Israel Ba'al was worshiped at local high places. He was symbolized by an uplifted stone. His consort is Asherah, symbolized by a carved stake symbolizing the tree of life.
      4. Several sources and types of idolatry are mentioned:
        1. the golden calves at Bethel and Dan set up by Jeroboam I to worship YHWH
        2. the worship of the Tyrian fertility god and goddess at local high places
        3. the necessary idolatry involved in political alliances of that day
          SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

    5. Political setting in the North
      1. Jeroboam II was the last strong king in Israel. He was fourth in the line of Jehu and the last one predicted to reign (cf. 2 Kgs. 10:30). He had a long and politically successful reign (786-746 B.C.)
      2. After the death of Jeroboam II there were six kings within a twenty-five year period.
        1. Zechariah (2 Kgs. 15:8-12). He was assassinated after only six months.
        2. Shallum (2 Kgs. 15:13-15). He was assassinated after only one month.
        3. Menahem (2 Kgs. 15:16-22). He reigned ten years, but paid heavy tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III.
        4. Pekahian (2 Kgs. 15:23-26). He reigned two years and was assassinated.
        5. Pekah (2 Kgs. 15:27-31). He reigned five years and was assassinated. He lost several cities to Assyria.
        6. Hoshea (2 Kgs. 15:3; 17:1-6). He reigned nine years and was exiled by Assyria in 722, when Samaria fell.
      3. Brief summary of the invasions of Assyria and Babylon during the eighth century which affected Palestine.
        1. The four eighth century prophets were active during the rise of the Tigris-Euphrates empire of Assyria. God would use this cruel nation to judge His people, particularly Israel. The specific incident was the formation of a trans-jordan political and military alliance known as the "Syro-Ephramatic League" (735 B.C.). Syria and Israel tried to force Judah to join them against Assyria. Instead Ahaz, king of Judah, sent a letter to Assyria asking for help. The first powerful empire-minded Assyrian king, Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 B.C.), responded to the military challenge and invaded Syria. Later, Assyria's puppet king, Hoshea (732-722 B.C.), in Israel, also rebelled, appealing to Egypt. Shalmaneser V (727-722 B.C.) invaded Israel again. He died before Israel was subdued, but his successor, Sargon II (722-705 B.C.), captured Israel's capital of Samaria in 722 B.C. Assyria deported over 27,000 Israelites on this occasion as Tiglath-Pileser had exiled thousands earlier in 732 B.C..
        2. After Ahaz's death (735-715 B.C.) another military coalition was formed by the trans-Jordan countries and Egypt against Assyria (714-711 B.C.). It is known as the "Ashdod Rebellion." Many Judean cities were destroyed when Assyria invaded again. Initially Hezekiah supported this coalition, but later withdrew his support.
        3. However, again, another coalition tried to take advantage of the death of Assyria's powerful king, Sargon II, in 705 B.C., along with the many other rebellions which occurred throughout the Assyrian Empire. Hezekiah fully participated in this rebellion. In light of this challenge Sennacherib (705-681 B.C.) invaded (701 B.C.) Palestine and camped near the city of Jerusalem (2 Kgs. 18-19; Isa. 36-39), but his army was miraculously destroyed by God. There is some question among scholars as to how many times Sennacherib invaded Palestine (e.g. John Bright has one invasion in 701 B.C. and another possible one in 688 B.C., cf. p. 270). Hezekiah was spared an Assyrian takeover, but because of his prideful exhibition of the treasures of Judah to the Babylonian delegation, Isaiah predicted Judah's fall to Babylon (39:1-8). Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 587-586 B.C.
        4. Isaiah also predicted the restoration of God's people under Cyrus II, the Medo-Persian ruler (Isa. 41:2-4; 44:28; 45:1; 56:11). Nineveh fell in 612 B.C. to Babylon, but the city of Babylon fell in 539 B.C. to Cyrus' army. In 538 B.C. Cyrus issued a decree that all exiled people, including the Jews, could return home. He even provided funds from his treasury for the rebuilding of the national temples.

  7. LITERARY UNITS

    1. Charges against the nations, Amos 1:1-2:3 (possibly through Amos 2:16)
      1. Syria (Damascus), Amos 1:3-5
      2. Philistia (Gaza), Amos 1:6-8
      3. Phoenicia (Tyre), Amos 1:9-10
      4. Edom, Amos 1:11-12
      5. Ammon, Amos 1:13-15
      6. Moab, Amos 2:1-3

    2. Special charges against God's people, Amos 2:4-6:14
      1. Judah, Amos 2:4-5
      2. Israel, Amos 2:6-6:14 (context of judgment on Israel through Amos 6:14)

    3. Visions of judgment, Amos 7:1-9:10
      1. Locusts, Amos 7:1-3
      2. Fire, Amos 7:4-6
      3. Plumb line, Amos 7:7-17
      4. Summer fruit, Amos 8:1-14
      5. Destruction of a sanctuary, Amos 9:1-10

    4. The Messianic hope, Amos 9:11-15
       Some scholars have suggested that this is not a "chronological structure," but a logical, literary structure (i.e. judgment ‒ restoration). Amos preached over a short period of time. The contents are his, but the structure may be an editor(s) preserving what was recorded of Amos' prophecies.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

  8. MAIN TRUTHS

    1. Amos relates YHWH's wrath to Israel's (and her neighbor's) violation of the Mosaic covenant. We need to realize the relationship between OT corporate (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE) responsibility and individual faith (cf. Ezek. 18:33). We have a societal sin problem as Israel did, however, in our minds, two standards often exist.
      1. our individual private lives and faith
      2. our corporate social, public lives 
         Israel must have rejoiced as Amos proclaimed YHWH's judgment on her surrounding neighbors (and traditional enemies). These nations were a part of the kingdoms of David and Solomon and must have known something of the Mosaic covenant and the God of Israel.
         The Israelites must have rejoiced indeed as Amos brought up God's judgment on her rival Judah (cf. Amos 2:4-5). But, the emotional affirmations quickly stopped when Amos, in a climactic fashion, turned to the sins of these northern tribes!
        SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

    2. God's sovereignty over all the earth is the background for YHWH's dealing in judgment with the nations outside the Covenant of Israel (see LXX of Deut. 32:8). This is the basis of Israel's understanding of monotheism (cf. Encyclopedia Judaica, vol. 2, p. 889).
       There are several texts that relate to YHWH's creation and control of nature (cf. Amos 4:13; 5:8-9; 8:8; 9:5-6). These form doxologies of praise! This book sees nature as a revelation of God (i.e. the earthquake, the eclipse, and the allusion to Deut. 27-29).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM
      SPECIAL TOPIC: NATURAL RESOURCES

    3. Amos 2:9-12, God's judgment against Israel, must be seen in the light of His gracious acts in history. YHWH's election and covenant with Israel sets the stage for His severe judgment. It must be remembered that "to whom much is given, much is required" (cf. Luke 12:48; Rom. 9:4-5).

    4. Amos 5 links faith and life inseparably! Amos denounces the wealthy's exploitation of the poor.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

    5. Israel was falsely trusting in:
      1. her religion, Amos 4:4-5; 5:21-23
      2. her economic prosperity, Amos 6:1ff
      3. her military power, Amos 2:14-16; 6:1b, 13

    6. Even amidst Israel's faithlessness there is hope in YHWH's covenant and Messiah, Amos 9:8b-15.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

* Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way. As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.

In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired—readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following SPECIAL TOPICS: Hebrew Grammatical Terms, Textual Criticism, and Glossary.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Chapters one and two form a literary unit dealing with the sins of the nations and of YHWH's covenant people. The first two verses could be the theme of the entire book. Israel's (i.e. the Northern Ten Tribes) unique relationship with YHWH causes them to be uniquely guilty of rebellion (cf. Rom. 9:4-5). They were Covenant People and they had a Covenant assignment.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

  2. Amos begins his Sermon with judgment on the enemies of Israel:
    1. all the surrounding nations
      1. pagans
      2. those related to the Jews
        (1) Edom by Esau
        (2) Ammon, Moab by Lot
    2. her kinsmen, Judea

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Amos 1:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 This begins the first poetic section in Amos. It is a summary of the entire book. See Introduction, VII.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "the Lord roars" The term "roars" (BDB 980, KB 1367, Qal IMPERFECT) was also used of YHWH's voice as thunder, Job 37:3-5 and Jer. 25:30. This seems to refer to His judgment (cf. Amos 3:8) based on Israel's sins amidst their covenantal knowledge (the nations mentioned were all part of David and Solomon's kingdoms and, therefore, had some knowledge of YHWH). This is similar to Joel 3:16.

The roar is the climactic moment of a lion's kill, the moment of judgment. It can refer to

  1. deliverance, as in Joel 3:16; Hosea 11:10
  2. but in this context of God's judgment

The Shepherd (Psalm 23:4c) has become the aggressive attacker! What a role reversal sin causes!!

For "Lord (YHWH)" see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "Zion. . .Jerusalem" These two names are in a synonymous, parallel relationship. The Israelites envisioned YHWH as symbolically dwelling between the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant in the Holy of Holies of the temple on Mt. Moriah in Jerusalem (cf. Exod. 25:22).

Jerusalem was built on seven hills.

  1. Mt. Zion was the hill on which the Jebusite citadel was located, which was not captured until David's day (cf. Josh. 15:63; 2 Sam. 5:6-10). David built his palace on this hill.
  2. Mt. Moriah was the hill on which the temple was built (cf. Gen. 22:2; 1 Chr. 21:1-22; 2 Chr. 3:1).

The mention of Jerusalem as the place from which YHWH roars was a subtle way to reject the golden calves which Jeroboam I set up at Bethel and Dan in Israel. YHWH dwelt in Judah's temple (cf. Amos 9:11), not Israel's shrines (cf. Amos 4:4; 5:5; 8:14)!

The original etymology of both "Zion" (BDB 851, KB 1022) and "Jerusalem" (BDB 436, KB 437) is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, ZION, JERUSALEM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ARK OF THE COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM

▣ "the shepherd's pasture grounds mourn, and the summit of Carmel dries up" YHWH's judgment on mankind's sin affects nature (cf. Genesis 3; Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; Romans 8:18-25; and the seals and bowls judgments of the book of Revelation). God uses nature to get mankind's attention (e.g. Amos 1:1c; 4:6-13; Ps. 19:1-6).

▣ "Carmel" Carmel was a mountain range in northern Israel that runs into the Mediterranean. It's name meant "vineyard of God" (BDB 501). It was proverbial for its lush vegetation (BDB 502) because it received so much annual rain.

entries.title: Amos 1:3 "Thus says the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "Thus says the Lord" This prophetic formula was a way of showing that the message was not the personal opinion of the prophet, but the very word of God. How much of the message was from the prophet (specific vocabulary, literary form) is uncertain. The mood or manner of inspiration is uncertain and may have variations, but the important truth is that it is a message from God. This message, though given in a certain language, historical situation, and culture, has a relevance to all cultures and times. Hermeneutically every passage has one meaning—that which the original inspired author meant to say—but many applications or significances related to the reader/hearer's historical and cultural situation. However, the application must be directly related to the original author's intent/message!

In this context the phrase announces the judgment of YHWH on nations and peoples (cf. Jer. 47:2; 48:1; Ezek. 25:3; 30:2; Amos 1:3; 2:1).

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "For three transgressions of Damascus and for four" This is a standard introductory phrase in Amos (cf. Amos 1:3,6,9,11,13; 2:1,4,6). It has also been found in other Near Eastern literature. It means that they sinned again and again.

The term "four" was used often in the Ancient Near East.

  1. four phases of the moon
  2. four divisions of the year (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 495)

In the OT itself it represented

  1. compass directions (i.e. a man facing east)
  2. wind directions (e.g. Dan. 7:2; 8:8)
  3. corners of the earth (e.g. Isa. 11:12)

From these came its implied meaning of completeness or fullness. Also the numbers three and four equals seven, which is another OT way to show completeness; the sins of these nations were full/complete!

The term "transgressions" (BDB 833, KB 981) is one of several Hebrew words which are used to describe sin and rebellion. In Amos this term takes on a sense of social sins (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 708). These nations rebel by attacking neighbors and relatives. Their actions show that they do not know YHWH. These nations were part of the Davidic empire and had been exposed to the worship of YHWH. These nations will be a part of a restored Davidic kingdom (cf. Amos 9:11-15; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)!

Prophets often spoke of YHWH's judgment on the nations (cf. Isa. 13-23; Jer. 46-51; Ezek. 25-32).

▣ "Damascus" The nation of Syria is also known as Aram with Damascus as its capital. The capital stands for the nation as a whole. It was besieged and captured by the Assyrian King Adad-Nirari III (796 B.C.), according to Assyrian Annals.

▣
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA  "I will not revoke its punishment"
NKJV, Peshitta  "I will not turn away its punishment"
TEV  "I will certainly punish them"
NJB  "I have made my decree and will not
  relent"
REB  "I will grant them no reprieve"
LXX  "I will not turn away from him"

The NEGATED VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is the usual VERB in the prophets to describe "repentance" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE [OT]). In this context the "I" refers to YHWH. The only vocabulary available to us to describe God relates to humans. God is an eternal Spirit. We use human words to describe Him (anthropomorphisms), but He is far beyond our ability to describe. However, He is affected by repentance and prayer (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE)

The question remains, "What is 'it' (see vv. 9,11,13)"? In context, it seems to refer to a common sense understanding of what is appropriate in human relations between nations.

  1. These surrounding nations had been under the influence of David and Solomon, therefore, they had some knowledge of YHWH's law.
  2. This refers to "natural revelation." See exegetical notes at Ps. 19:1-6 and also Rom. 1:18-23 (i.e. God known through nature); Rom. 2:14-15 (i.e. inner moral witness)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

▣ "they threshed Gilead with implements of sharp iron" "They" refers to the Syrians.

The VERB (BDB 190, KB 218,Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) refers to an agricultural procedure of separating grain from its husk (cf. Deut. 25:4; 2 Sam. 24:22; Isa. 28:28). It is used as imagery in 2 Kgs. 13:7; Isa. 21:10; Jer. 50:11; and Hosea 10:11. It is used of God's judgment (e.g. Micah 4:13 and Hab. 3:12).

Here it could also be imagery, but because of the Septuagint's translation of 2 Sam. 12:31, it may be literal. Whether figurative or literal, it speaks of Syrian abuses of Israelites (possibly related to 2 Kgs. 13:1-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "Gilead" This name (BDB 166) refers to the northern trans-jordan area between the Arnon and Jabbok Rivers that was given to the sons of Jacob, Reuben, and Gad. The specific atrocities of Syria (Aram) may relate to 2 Kgs. 8:28-29 or 10:32-33.

entries.title: Amos 1:3-2:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3-2:3 This is a literary unit which serves a theological purpose.

  1. YHWH is God of the whole earth (i.e. LXX of Deut. 32:8).
  2. All who sin must face His wrath.
  3. His people were grievously sinning, because they were covenant people and knew better (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

This unit must have been read or heard with glee as Israelites gladly welcomed God's judgment on these neighboring nations; yes, even Judah (cf. Amos 2:4-5). But suddenly, and surprisingly, Amos turns in climactic fashion, to Israel's sin (cf. Amos 2:6-6:14). Their prosperity, military power, and land expansion were not a sign of God's covenantal blessing (cf. Deuteronomy 27-29). Amos, the enforcer of Moses' Covenant, demands reckoning! The Day of the Lord would not be a blessing, but a curse (cf. Amos 5:18-20)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

1:2
NASB, NJB, LXX  "mourns. . .dries up"
NKJV, Peshitta  "mourn. . .withers"
NRSV  "wither. . .dries up"
REB  "dried up. . .parched"
TEV  "dry up. . .turn brown"
JPSOA  "languish. . .wither"
NET  "bellowing. . .wilt"

The first VERB (BDB 5, KB 6, Qal PERFECT with waw) seems to parallel the second VERB (BDB 386, KB 384, Qal PERFECT with waw). The problem is that the first VERB has such a large semantic field reflecting several different connotations to the root (אבל). It could denote "withering" or "mourning." Both fit usages in Amos. I think they are parallel.

entries.title: Amos 1:4 "I will send fire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4 "I will send fire" The VERB (BDB 1018, KB 1511, Piel PERFECT with waw), is parallel to "consume," "break," and "cut off." YHWH will destroy the fortifications and dynasty of the house of Hazael (Syria, Aram). Fire is a symbol of the judgment of God on wickedness (e.g. Isa. 30:27; Jer. 21:14; Ezek. 20:47-48; Zeph. 1:18; 3:8; Mal. 4:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "Hazael" This was the usurper monarch of Syria (BDB 303, cf. 2 Kgs. 8:7-15). He reigned from 843-796 B.C.(?). He was a powerful military adversary to Assyria's western expansion. Syria was invaded several times, but Damascus was not taken (i.e. 841, 837, and possibly 836 B.C.).

Once Assyrian pressure was lessened Hazael attacked his southern neighbors.

  1. trans-Jordan area, 2 Kgs. 10:32-33
  2. Philistia, 2 Kgs. 12:17
  3. Judah, 2 Kgs. 12:17-18

This reference is anachronism to an earlier title for Syria/Aram (i.e. "the House of Hazael").

▣ "citadels" The term (BDB 74) is translated in various ways:

  1. stronghold
  2. guardroom of the palace or temple
  3. fortress

The Akkadian loanword, b'rh, is used as a parallel in the Post-Exilic literature (e.g. of forts in 2 Chr. 17:12; 27:4 and of the temple in 1 Chr. 29:1; Neh. 2:8).

▣ "Ben-hadad" This (lit. "son of Hadad," BDB 122, cf. 2 Kgs. 13:3,24-25) is the "son of Hazael" (i.e. he reigned from 797-775 B.C.?). Probably his father gave him this name (in history as Ben Hadad III) because it became the common name (dynastic title) of many Syrian monarchs, like Pharaoh in Egypt or Caesar in Rome.

It is also possible that it reflects the worship of the storm god, Hadad (Ba'al or Rimmon, cf. 2 Kgs. 5:18). In this case it would be a condemnation on idolatry.

entries.title: Amos 1:5 "the gate bar of Damascus"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 "the gate bar of Damascus" Literally this refers to the lock on the main gate, a large wooden beam (or sometimes a metal bar, cf. 1 Kgs. 4:13), which was placed horizontally across two wooden doors. Symbolically, it refers to the destruction and exile of Syria (Aram) as a nation (cf. TEV).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NJB  "the inhabitant"
NRSV, TEV, Peshitta, JPSOA, LXX  "the inhabitants"
NIV  "the king"
NET  "the ruler"
JB  "the one enthroned"

This is a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE MASCULINE SINGULAR (BDB 442, KB 444, which means "to sit," "to dwell," or "to remain"). It is obvious there is a parallel between this term and the SINGULAR "him."

  1. Amos 1:5c, "him who holds the scepter"
  2. Amos 1:8b, "him who holds the scepter"

The Rotherham's Emphasized Bible has in the footnote, "him that is seated = that reigneth" (p. 873). Therefore, it seems that NIV, NET, JB have the contextual sense.

▣ "the Valley of Aven" The term "Aven" (BDB 20) can mean

  1. trouble
  2. sorrow
  3. wickedness
  4. idolatry

It is used in several ways in Amos-Hosea.

  1. a place of idolatry (here)
  2. a reference to Bethel by means of a Hebrew word play (cf. Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5,8)
  3. a reference to wickedness (cf. Hosea 6:8; 10:8; 12:11)
  4. nothingness (i.e. idolatry as vanity, cf. Amos 5:5)

Here, it refers to a place somewhere in Syria. The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, p. 284, notes that it is a Jewish word play on the city of Baalbek, which was called Heliopolis during the Greek period. McComiskey also asserts that because of the contact between Syria and Egypt this city may possibly have taken on the name of an Egyptian city, 'On (i.e. BDB 58 and the Septuagint, cf. Gen. 41:50; Exod. 30:17 and the Oxford NRSV Annotated Bible, p. 1171).

The site is geographically uncertain, but many believe that it refers to the Beqaa or Bekaa valley of Syria (i.e. the Septuagint).

▣ "him who holds the scepter" Originally the term "scepter" (BDB 986) referred to a wooden implement of war. Leaders were those who fought well. Here it refers to the Syrian king.

Their wooden weapon became a symbol of authority, rule, or power. It is used of

  1. the kings of pagan nations in Isa. 14:5; Amos 1:5,8; Zech. 10:11
  2. God's power in Isa. 10:5
  3. His Messiah's power in Isa. 11:4

▣ "Beth-eden" This name means "house of pleasure" (BDB 108 CONSTRUCT BDB 112). Its geographical location is uncertain, but may refer to

  1. a kingdom north of Aram on the bank of the Euphrates River in the time of Assurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III
  2. Baalbek in the Bukaa Valley in the time of Tiglath-pileser III
  3. simply sarcasm

▣ "So the people of Syria will be exiled to Kir" We learn from Amos 9:7 that this was their original homeland; they will be exiled to where they started from (BDB 885, cf. 2 Kgs. 16:9). However, its location is unknown. Most identify it as a location in Elam (cf. Isa. 22:6), but also possibly a region in northern Aram.

entries.title: Amos 1:6 "Gaza"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:6 "Gaza" This city (BDB 738) was a way of referring to the nation of Philistia. They were sea peoples from the Aegean Islands who tried to invade Egypt, but were defeated and settled on the southwestern coast of Palestine around 1200 B.C. They brought Iron Age technology with them and established control over a large area of the coastland. In Amos 1:6-8 four of their five major city-states are mentioned, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gaza (cf. Zeph. 2:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PHILISTINES

▣ "because they deported an entire population" Apparently the descendants of Esau were actively involved in purchasing Hebrew slaves taken by the Philistines (i.e. Ezek. 27:13). Entire communities were captured and sold (cf. Joel 3:3-8 and possibly 2 Chr. 21:16-17).

▣ "Edom" Edom, Moab, and Ammon were relatives of the Israelites. They lived in the southern trans-Jordan.

The JPSOA suggests an emendation to "Aram," both here and in v. 9.  Aram would denote Syria (i.e. Isa. 9:11).

  1. Edom ‒ אדם
  2. Aram ‒ ארם

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

entries.title: Amos 1:8 "him who holds the scepter"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 "him who holds the scepter" David Allan Hubbard, "Joel and Amos," Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, pp. 133 and 136), makes the historical point that Amos is accurate regarding:

  1. the Philistine cities were royal city-states surrounded by other cities ruled by those who bore the scepter of the city-state monarch (Amos 1:7)
  2. the Ammonites had a monarch and his officials (cf. Amos 1:15; Hosea 7:3,5,7,16; 8:4; see SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON)

▣ "the remnant of the Philistines will perish" The Philistines (BDB 814) were a traditional enemy of Judah from the time of Joshua to David. They will be completely destroyed as a nation and as a people.

▣ "My power" This is literally "I will turn My hand. . ." The VERB "turn" (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil PERFECT) has a wide semantic field. It is used often of repentance toward God or turning away from God. Here, it denotes God turning in judgment.

The term "hand" is imagery for power/action (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND). This particular phrasing is also used in Ps. 81:14; Isa. 1:25; Ezek. 38:12; Zech. 13:7.

Another common phrase is "to stretch out your hand/arm" (i.e. Jer. 6:12; 15:6; Ezek. 6:14; 14:9,13; 16:27; 20:33; 25:7,13,16; 35:3).

▣ "the Lord God" This is literally Adon YHWH. Since both are translated "lord," when they occur together YHWH is translated all capitals "God." The title is very common in Amos.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Amos 1:9 "Tyre"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:9 "Tyre" This (BDB 862) refers to the nation of Phoenicia, which seems to have been made up racially of Canaanites and the Sea Peoples (Aegean Sea). This nation became the source of the fertility worship of both Ba'al and Asherah, which permeated the Northern Ten Tribes through the influence of Jezebel (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:31-33; 18:19,21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "I will not revoke its punishment" This parallels vv. 3,11,13. See note at v. 3.

▣ "because they delivered up an entire population to Edom" Homer mentions Tyre's slave trade in his Odyssey 4:288ff; 15:473ff.

▣ "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood" This refers to some type of treaty, possibly the precedent of one that was made with Solomon (cf. 2 Sam. 5: 11; 1 Kgs. 5:1-18; 9: 11- 14). It also may refer to the unnatural behavior of selling one's neighbor (i.e. blood relative) into slavery. All of the sins mentioned in this section deal with mankind's inhumanity toward his fellowman. Phoenicia not only violated YHWH's laws, it violated the common mores of the ANE.

entries.title: Amos 1:10 "I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:10 "I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre,

 And it will consume her citadels" Tyre (capital of Phoenicia) was an island fortress that was almost impregnable. However, during Alexander the Great's move through Palestine in 332 B.C., after a seven-month siege, the city fell when the enemy built a causeway out of the rubble of the destroyed mainland city. We learn from historical documents that 6,000 were killed, 2,000 were crucified or impaled and 30,000 were sold into slavery.

Nebuchadnezzar II never took the island citadel, but after many years, it surrendered by treaty.

entries.title: Amos 1:11 "Edom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:11 "Edom" This (BDB 10) refers to near relatives of the Israelites through Esau, Gen. 25:19-26; 36:1-19. Edom and Israel were always at odds. Edom becomes a symbol of broken family bonds and covenants. She is often condemned in the prophets (cf. Isa. 34:5-17; 63:1-6; Jer. 49:7-22; Lam. 4:21-22; Ezek. 25:12-14; 35:1-15; Mal. 1:2-4).

Petra was its capital (cf. Ps. 137:7; Ezek. 25:12-14; Obad. vv. 10-15; Mal. 1:2-4). It was located east of Judah in the trans-Jordan region (modern Jordan).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

▣ "I will not revoke its. . ." This is a parallel phrase with no stated object, vv. 3,13. See note at v. 3.

▣
NASB  "compassion"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "pity"
TEV  "mercy"
REB  "natural affections"

This term (BDB 933) can also refer to a treaty partner (i.e. "ally," NIV footnote and NET Bible), thereby parallel to "brother" in line d.

The LXX follows a different ancient Hebrew text, "and he spoiled a womb upon the ground and seized his shivering fight for a testimony."

▣ "His anger also tore continually,

And he maintained his fury forever"

These two poetic lines are parallel. "His anger" refers to the settled, continual anger of the Edomites against the Israelis. The PRONOUNS in this verse are ambiguous. They refer to two different subjects.

  1. YHWH ‒ line c
  2. Edom/Aram ‒ line b, d-e
  3. Lines f, g could refer to either one, but the parallelism seems to prefer #2 in the last two poetic lines.

Again, God's judgment comes because of sins against people, in this case relatives (option #1 above).

The VERB "tore" (BDB 382, KB 380, Qal IMPERFECT) is used of lions tearing apart their prey (i.e. Ps. 7:2; Ezek. 22:25). Notice YHWH is characterized as a lion in v. 2. Here, Edom's sins against humanity are characterized with the same violent VERB.

The JPSOA on the last line of poetry in v. 11 has, "And his fury stormed unchecked." This is an emendation from the MT.

  1. MT ‒ שׁמר, denoting "guard" (BDB 1036, KB 1581)
  2. Akkadian root ‒ שמר, denoting "anger," thereby a better poetic parallel to line 4

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER, PERPETUITY (BDB 664, KB 773)

entries.title: Amos 1:12 "Teman"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:12 "Teman" This (BDB 412) was a northern district of Edom (cf. Jer. 49:7,20; Obad. 9) whose capital was Bozrah.

▣ "Bozrah" This (BDB 131) refers to one of the larger northern cities of Edom located at a major oasis on "the King's Highway" (trans-Jordan trade route from the Gulf of Aqaba north to Damascus). It was a city of great antiquity (cf. Gen. 36:33; 1 Chr. 1:44). It will be destroyed by YHWH (cf. Jer. 49:13).

entries.title: Amos 1:13 "Ammon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 "Ammon" This (BDB 769) is also a relative of the Israelis through Lot (cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The Israelites were not to confront them on their exodus because they were relatives (cf. Deut. 2:19). Ammon was located in the trans-jordan area between the Arnon and Jabbok Rivers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON

▣ "Because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead" Gilead (BDB 166) is in the northern trans-jordan area. There is no historical reference to this specific act, but this practice was well known (cf. 2 Kgs. 8:12; 15:16; Hosea 13:16). However, the judgment of YHWH falls on all of these nations because of their violent war practices.

The NET Bible, p. 1590, # 11, suggests that "brother" (BDB 26) in v. 11, comes from the word "womb" and, therefore, may refer to the slaughter of women (cf. LXX of v. 11). If so, verse 13 is a parallel of the horrible acts of these other ANE nations.

▣ "In order to enlarge their borders" This slaughter of innocent women and children was not related to holy war, as was the Israeli attack on Jericho (cf. Joshua 6), but was simply motivated by greed for more land.

entries.title: Amos 1:14 "Rabbah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:14 "Rabbah" This term means "the great" (BDB 913). This title was used of a city of Ammon, located at the headwaters of the Jabbok River (cf. Deut. 3:11; 2 Sam. 12:26; 17:27), which served as the captial of Ammon.

▣
NASB, NJB, REB  "war cries"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "shouting"
LXX  "a cry on the day of battle"

This term (BDB 929) has a large semantical field:

  1. raise a shout
    1. for attack
    2. for victory
    3. for worship
    4. for destruction
  2. give a blast

Often a battle cry is linked to a trumpet blast, as in Josh. 6:5,10,16,20. Every nation had its own war cry (cf. Amos 2:2; 1 Sam. 17:20,52, also see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 9,254). Israel's was linked to YHWH (cf. Jdg. 7:20-21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

entries.title: Amos 2:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 The literary judgment form (i.e. funeral dirge) of chapter one continues through chapter two (cf. Amos 1:3; see notes there).

▣ "Moab" These were also relatives of the Israelis through Lot (cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The country is in the trans-jordan area just north of Edom between the Arnon and Zered Rivers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

▣ "because he burned the bones of the king of Moab to lime" These actions, of which we have no biblical or archaeological information, involved

  1. opening the grave
  2. removing the remains
  3. burning them
  4. mixing them to make mortar (i.e. for buildings) or plaster (i.e. for whitewashing walls)

These actions were seen as a way to humiliate and to affect negatively one's place/rest in the afterlife (i.e. 2 Kgs. 23:16-20; Isa. 33:12). This purposeful violation of that which was culturally sacred and taboo shows the level of animosity. This does not refer to cremation as a way of disposing of a dead body, but to a later desecration! It does, however, give me a chance to discuss modern concerns about cremation (see Special Topic below).

Cremation was an abominable practice to all the Near Eastern people. It is only mentioned in the Bible in connection with great crimes (cf. Gen. 28:24; Lev. 20:14; 21:9; Josh. 7:15,25). Apparently out of hatred Moab burned the king of Edom's bones and mixed them with mortar to build buildings or plaster to whitewash walls (Targums). Lime (BDB 966, cf. Isa. 33:12) was an ingredient of mortar and plaster (whitewash).

It is possible that this act is imagery for complete destruction (i.e. Vulgate). It is difficult to interpret VERBS that have both literal and figurative uses. This is especially true of poetic passages, as the book of Amos.

The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 766, mentions that the only piece of information about this general period comes from the Mesha Inscription. The problem is this relates to the 9th century B.C. and our current text is related to the 8th century B.C. The Assyrian King Tiglath-Pileser III conquered this transJordan area in 734 B.C.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Amos 2:2 "I will send fire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:2 "I will send fire" This phrase refers to

  1. YHWH's judgment
  2. the literal burning of cities

It is a recurrent phrase in Amos 1:4,7,10,12,14; 2:2,5 and Hosea 8:14. Fire is often sent as

  1. a cleansing agent
  2. a symbol of God's presence
  3. a means of judgment

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "the citadels" See note at Amos 1:4.

▣ "Kerioth" This (BDB 90, KB 1142) is a region's or city's name. The NEB, following the LXX, translated it as "towns" (because of the DEFINITIVE ARTICLE, cf. Jer. 48:41), but the revision of the NEB, called the REB, puts the place name back into the translation (i.e. "the palaces of Kerioth"). This city is also mentioned in Jer. 48:24,41. This city (possibly Kir, cf. Isa. 15:1) had a major shrine to the Moabite fertility god, Chemosh (cf. The Mesha Stone L.12; 1 Kgs. 11:33).

The UBS Text Project, p. 277, gives "Kerioth" a "B" rating. The difference is only vocalization.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHEMOSH

▣ "with war cries" See note at Amos 1:14. War cries and trumpet blasts are often used as signals in battle. The phrase in some contexts refers to the sound of confusion and fear during battle.

▣ "the sound of the trumpet" Trumpets were used to direct troops in the field. See note at Amos 1:14.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

entries.title: Amos 2:3 "the judge"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:3 "the judge" This is used in the sense of monarch. The king acted as judge (cf. Micah 5:2), as God's representative (cf. Gen. 18:25; Jdg. 11:27; Ps. 50:6; 75:7; 94:2; Isa. 33:22). The parallel phrase, "all her princes," refers to the royal family. Moab will be totally destroyed as a nation (cf. Mal. 1:2-5).

entries.title: Amos 2:4 "Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "Judah" The charges against Judah are theological (rejection of YHWH's covenant, i.e. Mosaic Laws) not just violent acts against other people groups/relatives. The charges would have been denied by Judah, but apparently the same sins against YHWH which characterized Israel were also committed by Judah (cf. Jer. 3:6-10; Ezek. 23:1-49).

▣ "they rejected the law of the Lord" The VERBAL "rejected" (BDB 549, KB 540, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used in two seemingly opposite senses (i.e. conditional covenant, see SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT):

  1. to reject or refuse someone or something (i.e. here, God's law)
  2. for God refusing to reject His people. They reject Him and His covenant, prophets, and worship, but He, the covenant God, punishes them but does not fully reject them.

The paradox is clearly seen in a series of texts from Jer. 6:30; 7:29; 14:19; and 31:37! In Amos (cf. Amos 2:4; 5:21) and Hosea (cf. Hosea 4:6 [twice]; 9:17) YHWH rejects a generation of His people because of their willful rejection of Him and His law (cf. Hosea 4:6; 8:1,12)! All of Israel's descendants were never right with God, only those who exercised faith, repentance, and obedience!

I have come to believe that the longsuffering of YHWH towards the seed of Abraham ended in A.D. 70 with the Roman destruction of the temple. The Mosaic covenant has been filled and universalized by the new covenant brought about in Jesus (i.e. Matt. 5:17-20,21-48).

I believe that Jesus' Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21) and Paul's "the man of lawlessness" (i.e. 2 Thess. 2), as well as the book of Revelation, describes this A.D. 70 "coming" of Jesus.

This view of eschatology is called Partial-Preterism. Please see my exegetical, verse-by-verse commentary on these passages free online.

▣ "law. . .statutes" These are the Hebrew terms

  1. law ‒ BDB 435
  2. statutes ‒ BDB 349

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

▣ "their lies also have led them astray" This term "lies" (BDB 469) means "lie," "falsehood," or "deceptive thing." NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 619, characterizes it well, "emphasizes an action or word that is false, a lie, because it somehow violates God's character, word, or deed, as expressed in himself, his prophet or his creations." Psalm 40:5 and the NIV reflect this concept. The "lies" refer to false teaching and the worship of false gods (cf. Hab. 2:18).

This same concept is carried over in the NT where in 1 John the "lie" refers to unbelief in Jesus, the ultimate sin and covenant incompatibility.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

▣ "their fathers walked" This is an idiomatic way of asserting that this generation, as well as previous generations, faithfully worshiped the fertility gods of Canaan (i.e. Ba'al and Asherah/Astarte).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Amos 2:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:5 This is a reference to the Neo-Babylonian Exile that will befall Judah in the days ahead (i.e. 586 B.C.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON, D.

entries.title: Amos 2:6 "Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6 "Israel" Amos got the attention of his audience by first proclaiming judgment against the surrounding enemies, then their anticipation was hightened by proclaiming judgment on Israel's covenant brothers (Judah), but now he shocked them by turning to God's judgment on them!

The northern group of tribes that split from the southern group in 922 B.C. was called by several names.

  1. the northern ten tribes
  2. Israel (the collective name)
  3. Samaria (the captial city)
  4. Ephraim (the largest tribe)

This northern group of tribes included all except

  1. Judah
  2. Simeon
  3. Benjamin
  4. most Levites

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "Because they sell the righteous for money" Because of the allusion to the purchase of slaves by Edom from/to the Philistines (cf. Amos 1:6), and the Phoenicians (cf. Amos 1:9), this is probably a reference to selling their countrymen into slavery. The term "sell" (BDB 569, KB 581, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used in two senses:

  1. persons kidnaped to be sold as slaves
  2. to sell oneself to a creditor for a period of time

It is certain that this is a reference against those who were wealthy, who abused the socially ostracized and needy (cf. Prov. 14:31; 17:5; Micah 2:1-3).

The term "righteous" here is used in parallel with

  1. "the needy" (Amos 2:6)
  2. "the helpless" (Amos 2:7)
  3. "the humble" (Amos 2:7)

So in this context (and remember context determines meaning) it does not have a theological orientation, but a social one. Righteous people are related to YHWH and His law and thereby treat their covenant partners appropriately. Righteousness in Amos has a vertical and a horizontal aspect. In Hosea the term takes on a more religious (theological or vertical aspect) orientation (cf. Hosea 2:19; 10:12; 14:9. In context it is often related to hesed (i.e. covenant faithfulness; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS).

Because this context has a legal/judicial flavor, the term probably refers to the defendant in a legal trial who cannot afford to bribe the judge (i.e. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 16:19; Prov. 17:23; Isa. 1:23; 5:21; Jer. 5:28; Micah 3:11; 7:3)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "And the needy for a pair of sandals" This may be interpreted literally as meaning

  1. people bought and sold for a very small amount (cf. Amos 8:5-6)
  2. a court procedure (i.e. the exchanging of shoes, cf. Ruth 4:7, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, p. 169) to give some legality to these scandalous enslaving practices of the rich.
  3. The NET Bible, p. 1592, #24, mentions a possible textual emendation.
    1. נעלים ‒ BDB 653, "shoes"
    2. עלם ‒ KB 834 I, "hidden," referring to a bribe

The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 228, has a significant statement related to the social concept of "needy," "poor," and "poverty."

"Where western thinking stresses the economic aspect of poverty, the ANE understood poverty in the context of shame and honor. So the possession of land, power, economic security, and social states made a person rich, and the absence of these factors made a person poor."

2:7
NASB, NKJV  "pant"
NRSV, TEV, JPSOA  "trample"
NJB  "crushed"
REB  "grind"
LXX  "tread on"
Peshitta  "oppress"

There is much discussion about the translation of this term (BDB 983, KB 1375, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) in Amos 2:7:

  1. the NASB and NKJV imply that the rich begrudged (i.e. "gasp for air" KB 1375 or "pant after" BDB 983 I, e.g. Job 7:2; Ps. 119:131; Eccl. 1:5) the small amount of dust the poor placed on their heads in mourning (hyperbole)
  2. the NRSV, following the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and JPSOA, translates this term "to crush" or "to trample" (BDB 983 II, e.g. 8:4; Ps. 56:2; Ezek. 36:3), which seems to imply the affluent's humiliation and domination of the poor.

In this context "the righteous," "the needy," "the helpless," and "the humble" refer not to the perennially poor, but the recently exploited middle class farmers or merchants who had been forced to borrow money and thereby lost their tribal lands, income, pride, and social position. For a good discussion of the rich and poor in the OT see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 72-74. Because of the term's use in Amos 8:4 the second option seems best.

▣
NASB, LXX  "turn aside the way of the humble"
NKJV  "pervert the way of the humble"
NRSV, REB  "push the afflicted out of the way"
TEV  "push the poor out of the way"
NJB  "thrust the rights of the oppressed to one side"
REB  "push the humble out of the way"
JPSOA  "make the humble walk a twisted course"
Peshitta  "turn away justice from the fatherless"

The VERB (BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is used several times in Amos.

  1. In Amos 2:7 and 5:12 it refers to abuses of the legal system caused by the wealthy's bribery of the judges (e.g. Exod. 23:6; Deut. 16:19; 24:17; 27:19; 1 Sam. 8:3; Prov. 17:23; Isa. 10:2; Lam. 3:35).
  2. In Amos 2:8 it refers to the wealthy reclining on the garments taken from the poor as pledges for a debt.

The basic meaning of the term is to "stretch out" or "spread out." In the first example above the judges stretched out their hands for a bribe. In the second example the garments of the poor are spread out so that the wealthy can sit on them or possibly lie on them, which could even imply cultic prostitution.

▣ "a man and his father resort to the same girl" The term for girl (BDB 655) here is not the normal term for cult prostitute, although that may be what this is referring to (cf. Deut. 23:18; for historical setting see Hosea 4:12-14). It could also refer to the "selling" of a poor, young maiden, whereby she would be used as a concubine by all the men in one family (cf. TEV). This would violate

  1. Lev. 18:8; 20:11; Deut. 22:30; 27:20
  2. Exod. 21:7-11

Since the context is the abuse of the poor and helpless, then the second option seems best.

There have been several other interpretations (see NET Bible, p. 1593, #2). One cannot be specific about the precise nature of some of these violations, but the overall context is very clear. Humans, even covenant people, are sinful and violate God's laws! YHWH does not take sin and sinners lightly, especially those who should have known Him (i.e. Judah and Israel, cf. Rom. 9:4-5). We reap what we sow in direct proportion to the light (and power) we have (see full list of texts at Gal. 6:7-10)!

▣ "In order to profane My holy name" These acts were flaunted at the shrines (golden calves of Jeroboam II) at Bethel and Dan (cf. Amos 2:8). They had the appearance of legality and religious approval, but everyone knew what was happening!

This VERBAL (BDB 320 III, KB 319, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used in several senses in the Piel form:

  1. to defile sexually, Lev. 19:29; 21:9,15
  2. to defile ceremonially, Lev. 19:8; 21:12,23; 22:9,15
  3. to defile YHWH's name, Lev. 18:21; 19:12; 20:3; 21:6; 22:2,32; Jer. 34:16; Ezek. 20:39; 36:20-23; Amos 2:7

The cultic acts of the Israelites were polluting, defiling, and profaning the very God they claimed to worship and serve (cf. Ezek. 36:22-32)! They flagrantly ignored the Mosaic legislation for personal gain and pleasure!

It is obvious that Amos (like all of the prophets) judged actions in light of the Mosaic Law (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT]).

  1. Amos 2:4 uses the terms "the law of the Lord" and "His statutes" to refer to the Mosaic legislation (see SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION).
  2. Amos 2:7 relates to Lev. 18:8,15; 20:11-12
  3. Amos 2:8 relates to Deut. 24:12-13
  4. Amos 2:9-11 relates to Gen. 15:12-21
  5. Amos 2:11-12 relates to Numbers 6

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

entries.title: Amos 2:8 "On the garments taken as pledges they stretch out beside every altar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "On the garments taken as pledges they stretch out beside every altar" The rich were taking and keeping (prohibited in Exod. 22:26-27; Deut. 24:12-13; Job 22:6) the sleeping garments (outer cloaks) of the poor as a pledge for loans (see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, p. 171; cf. Exod. 21:7,26-28; Lev. 25:39-40; Deut. 24:10-13,17; Prov. 20:16; 27:13). This may relate to cultic prostitution mentioned in Amos 2:7 or a cultic meal connected to the worship of fertility gods.

The phrase, "every altar," shows the idolatrous nature of the worship being offered to Ba'al (male) and Asherah (female), who were local fertility gods with an altar in each and every community. YHWH had only one official altar (i.e. Mt. Moriah). Jeroboam I had established two alternate sites at Bethel and Dan to prevent his people (i.e. the northern tribes) from returning to Jerusalem for feast days.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FEASTS OF ISRAEL

▣ "in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined" There are two possible interpretations:

  1. in the cultic centers of Dan and Bethel the rich were becoming intoxicated on the revenue they illegally extracted from the poor
  2. the temple taxes were being used to promote drunkenness and sexual practices

Some translations translate Elohim as "their gods" or "their god" (NJB, NAB, NIV), but the context implies a reference to YHWH (NASB, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, NET). See SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

This is not a condemnation of wine, but of its abuse.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM

entries.title: Amos 2:9-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:9-12 This is a historical rendition of the gracious acts of YHWH during the Conquest, which sets the stage for Israel's judgment. God's people's violations of His covenant are not new, but perennial (cf. Nehemiah 9; Acts 7).

entries.title: Amos 2:9 "it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 "it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them" This is "holy war" terminology referring to YHWH fighting on behalf of His people (notice the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR PRONOUN in Amos 2:9,10.13). The victory belonged to Him (e.g. "hornets," Exod. 23:28; Deut. 7:20; Josh. 24:12; "hail stones," Josh. 10:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMORITE

▣ "though his height" This may simply be imagery for power (BDB 147) using trees (cedars can grow up to 100' high; see SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES) or possibly a literal reference to the physical height of some of the Amorites, Og of Bashan and the Anakim of Hebron (cf. Num.13:28, 33; Deut. 1:28; 9:2; Josh. 11:21-22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

▣ "I even destroyed his fruit above and his root below" This is an idiom or proverb of total destruction, here used of the Amorite people. Verses 9-10 draw imagery from the period of the Exodus and Conquest.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMORITE

entries.title: Amos 2:10 "It was I who brought you up from the land of Egypt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 "It was I who brought you up from the land of Egypt" The deliverance was prophesied to Abraham (cf. Gen. 15:12-21). This special covenant relationship with the descendants of the Patriarchs is affirmed by the national group in Exod. 19-20. But collectively they turned away and rejected YHWH's covenant (cf. Hosea 13:4-6). Israel was more responsible because she had so much more spiritual light (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "I led you in the wilderness forty years" This is a reference to the wilderness wandering period. The term "forty" is a round number in the OT. Here it refers to the thirty eight years of travel from Kadesh-Barnea to the Promised Land (by way of the trans-Jordan).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (uncertainties)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

▣ "That you might take possession of the land of the Amorite" This refers to YHWH's promise to Abraham in Gen. 15:12-21. Notice the term "Amorite" refers to

  1. all of the land of Canaan in Amos 2:16
  2. one of several indigenous tribes in Amos 2:21

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

entries.title: Amos 2:11 "Is this not so"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:11 "Is this not so" YHWH challenges them to affirm the trustworthiness of His words of condemnation. But this is also a sorrowful, personal message from their God! The phrase "sons of Israel" has Abrahamic covenant implications. God still loves and cares for His people (His true people reflect His character!).

▣ "declares the Lord" This is a special phrase to denote God's revelation (cf. Amos 2:11, 16; 3:10,13,15; 4:1,5-6, 8-11; 6:6, 14; 9:7-8,12,13).

entries.title: Amos 2:11-12 "I raised up some of your sons to be prophets. . .Nazirites"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:11-12 "I raised up some of your sons to be prophets. . .Nazirites" YHWH's special choice of these spiritual leaders showed His special care for Israel. But Israel caused these men (and possibly women, cf. Num. 6:2) to sin (cf. Amos 2:12). They were God's gift, but His people perverted their giftedness!

"Nazirites" are described in Numbers 6. They could be male or female (cf. Num. 6:2). There were several unique guidelines for their calling to continue:

  1. cannot eat any product from the grapevine, Num. 6:3-4
  2. cannot cut his/her hair, Num. 6:5
  3. cannot touch a dead body (i.e. funerals of loved ones), Num. 6:6-7

This special vow (temporary [e.g. Num. 6:13-20; Acts 18:18; 21:23] or life long [Jdg.13:7; 1 Sam. 1:1; Luke 7:33]) was a way for people who were not priests or Levites to dedicate themselves to YHWH in a special sense! It is also significant that in a male-dominated culture ancient Israelites allowed female Nazirites (and prophetesses).

For a good brief discussion see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 2, pp. 466-467.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAZIRITE VOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Amos 2:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12 The evil of God's people is exemplified by

  1. Nazirites ‒ drink
  2. prophets ‒ can not speak

This represents a total reversal in God's clearly revealed will for His people.

entries.title: Amos 2:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 There are two ways to understand this verse.

  1. It refers to YHWH being weighed down (as an overloaded wagon) by His people's sin (from Arabic root, cf. Isa. 43:24; and the NASB, NKJV, NET, NIV, REB translations).
  2. It refers to YHWH "pressing down" (i.e. judging) His people (from Arabic root, cf. Isa. 28:27-28; and the NRSV, TEV, NJB).
  3. JPSOA
    1. in text, "I will slow your movements, as a wagon is slowed, when full of grain"
    2. in footnote, "I will slow your movements, as a threshing sledge is slowed, when clogged by cut grain"

The differences relate to which root the VERBS derive (BDB 734, KB 802, Hiphil PARTICIPLE and Hiphil IMPERFECT). In this case certainty is impossible (NET Bible gives four possible roots, p. 1593, #14).

The UBS, A Translator's Handbook on the Book of Amos, suggests a translation that follows option #2, where the people of Israel groan under God's judgment like an overloaded cart, pp. 55-56. This series of grammar focused information is very helpful. I commend it to you!

entries.title: Amos 2:14-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:14-16 This described the panicked retreat of the Israeli army before the Assyrians. YHWH had been with them in the Exodus and Conquest, but now His presence was for judgment, not deliverance! He strikes fear and panic into the hearts of Israel's best soldiers. This is an exact reversal of "Holy War"!

2:14,15
NASB, NJB, JPSOA  "life"
NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "himself"
NRSV, TEV  "lives"
LXX  "soul"

The MT has nephesh (BDB 659) which denotes a whole person.

Humans do not have a "soul" (i.e. Greek thought), they are a soul (Hebrew thought, cf. Gen. 2:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Amos 2:16 "the warriors will flee naked"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:16 "the warriors will flee naked" This idiomatic phrase refers to the throwing off of all armor and all unnecessary clothing so that the soldiers could retreat even faster (JPSOA, "unarmed," but footnote, "naked").

▣ "in that day" This phrase, "in that day" or "on that day," is a way for the eighth century prophets to speak of YHWH's visitation (presence), both for judgment and restoration (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY).

This pattern is typical of the prophets. God is going to act against sin in time, but He also offers a day of repentance and forgiveness to those who change their hearts and actions! God's purpose of redemption and restoration will be accomplished! He will have a people who reflect His character. The purpose of creation (fellowship between YHWH and humanity) will be fulfilled (see SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "declares the Lord"
NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "says the Lord"

This literary unit (Amos 1:3-2:16) repeats the term "says" (BDB 55, KB 65, Qal PERFECT), showing that these judgments are from YHWH, not Amos. This phrase can introduce or conclude a prophetic literary unit.

A parallel form (BDB 610 and 217 CONSTRUCT) is in Amos 2:11 and 2:16 (e.g. Amos 3:13; 4:3; 6:8,14; 8:3,9,11). Amos believed that YHWH Himself had spoken a clear message to him and he faithfully passes it on.

entries.title: Amos 3:1 "Hear"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 "Hear" This is the Hebrew VERB Shema (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE), which means "to hear so as to do" (e.g. Deut. 5:1; 6:4; 9:1). It may be used in this section of Amos to mark transition to a new topic (i.e. Amos 3:1,13; 4:1; 5:1,23; 7:16; 8:4; Hosea 4:1; 5:1; Micah 1:2; 3:1; 6:1).

Knowledge of YHWH always involves obedience (cf. Amos 3:1,13; 4:1; 5:1; 8:4). There are covenant benefits and requirements (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "which the Lord has spoken against you, sons of Israel, against the entire family" Amos has set up this condemnation of Israel by first condemning the surrounding nations, even Judah!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name), II. D.

▣
MT, NASB  "sons of Israel"
NKJV, Peshitta  "O children of Israel"
NRSV, JPSOA  "O people of Israel"
TEV, REB  "the entire nation"
NJB  "Israelites"
LXX  "O household of Israel"

There is a purposeful ambiguity in this phrase. In one sense it refers to all the tribes of Israel, but in another, to the Northern Ten Tribes who split away under Jeroboam I in 922 B.C. Verse 2 obviously includes all descendants of the Patriarchs.

The break away northern tribes go by several names during this period of history (i.e. 922-722 B.C.).

  1. collective term ‒ Israel
  2. name of their capital city ‒ Samaria
  3. name of the largest tribe ‒ Ephraim
  4. a number designation, "the Northern Ten" tribes

 However, this numerical idiom is literary, not literal.

  1. southern tribes had four tribes (counting the majority of Levites and priests)
    1. Judah
    2. Simeon
    3. Benjamin
    4. most Levites
  2. northern tribes had nine tribes and some Levites and priests

▣ "against the entire family" One reason modern western people misunderstand the OT is its focus on corporality, while most westerners focus on individuals. The ancient people lived or died together. They lived for the good of the aggregate.

It is hard for moderns to fathom this sense of corporality. It involves corporate sin and guilt, but not corporate righteousness. Righteousness was an individual matter of faith, repentance, obedience, worship, and perseverance. God's judgment of His people impacted both the sinful and innocent.

If this concept is brought over into today, it would require an understanding that humans are responsible for their personal relationship to God, as well as sharing the corporate guilt of their societies! Sin is both commission and omission. It also implies there are national, temporal judgments, which are designed (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29) to cause sinners to turn or return to God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

▣ "which he brought up from the land of Egypt" The VERB (BDB 748, KB 828) is a Hiphil PERFECT. The Exodus experience is the first national event for descendants of Abraham (cf. Gen. 15:12-21; Amos 2:10; 9:7). YHWH was faithful, but this was matched by the continual unfaithfulness of the descendants of the Patriarchs (both Israel and Judah, i.e. "the entire family," cf. Nehemiah 9; Acts 7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "land" Notice the term here used of Egypt is erets (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH), but in 3:2, the term is adamah (BDB 9), used for Israel (see SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD [several terms]). It is difficult to know when they are synonymous (i.e. literary variety) or used in a special sense. Only context can determine!
