FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Amos 5:2 "she has fallen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2 "she has fallen" This (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECT) is a PROPHETIC PERFECT that describes something that will happen in the future as if it has already occurred. The term was used of death in battle (e.g. Jer. 9:22; 46:12; Lam. 2:21; Hosea 7:7).

▣ "she will not rise again" There are two VERBS:

  1. "no more" (BDB 414, KB 418 is a Hiphil IMPERFECT)
  2. "to rise" (BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

YHWH's judgment on Israel's eclectic religion is total, complete, once-and-for-all judgment (cf. Amos 4:11; 7:9).

However, this very same VERB is used in Amos 9:11(twice) to promise a restoration of the royal house of Judah (i.e. "the fallen booth of David"). So again, the theological issue is:

  1. YHWH's message presented in contrasting black and white truths (dialectic paradoxes)
  2. chapter 9 refers only to Judah, not Israel

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "the virgin Israel" This term is parallel with "house of Israel." YHWH took special care and provided protection for them, like an unmarried daughter (cf. Jer. 14:17) or bride to be (cf. Jer. 18:13; 31:4,21). This reflects the marriage imagery for YHWH as husband and His covenant people as wife (e.g. Isa. 54:5; Hosea 2:19; Eph. 5:22-33). The later rabbis saw the wilderness wandering period as their honeymoon (cf. Jer. 2:2-3; Hosea 2:16). But now the context is of the rape and death of Israel by Assyrian invasion.

For more information on this idiom, see Jer. 46:11 online at www.freebiblecommentary.org.

▣ "She lies neglected on her land" The VERB (BDB 643, KB 695, Niphal PERFECT) means forsaken, abandoned to plunder. The land of promise is now the place of judgment.

There is a very interesting article in NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 522-524, on the theological aspect of "the land" as YHWH's gift to the descendants of Abraham (cf. Gen. 12:3; 15:12-21). Many of the Mosaic statutes are based on this concept. This is the reason why cheating fellow covenant brothers out of their family/tribal inheritance was so offensive to YHWH. YHWH's concern for the land can be seen in "the Sabbath Year" and "Jubilee Year" regulations. These wealthy land grabbers had totally ignored or willfully rejected the theological basis of YHWH's ownership and division of the Promised Land (ie. Josh. 12-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL II. C.

▣ "There is none to raise her up" This is the same VERBAL (BDB 877, KB 1086, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) used earlier in the verse (Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT). It seems to be a sarcastic allusion to the inability of the Canaanite gods (whom Israel worshiped) to rescue her from YHWH's judgment (cf. Amos 5:6). The powerlessness, the non-existence of Canaanite deities is ridiculed!

entries.title: Amos 5:3 "the Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:3 "the Lord God" This title, "Adon YHWH,' appears often in Amos.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ This was one of the covenant curses (the terms "thousands" [BDB 48] and "hundreds" [BDB 547] were military units). The emphasis in this verse is not on a remnant returning (cf. Isa. 6:13), but on the extreme military devastation that will occur.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

entries.title: Amos 5:4 "seek Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:4 "seek Me" The Hebrew VERB (BDB 205, KB 233) is a Qal IMPERATIVE (cf. Amos 5:6,14-15). The connotation of the Hebrew phrase "to seek" involved going to a sanctuary, however, the context of Amos 5:5 demands that we must seek God on an individual, as well as corporate, basis (cf. Deut. 4:29), not just in religious ritual. Our attitudes, motives, and lifestyle faith are crucial. Basically this is a call to repentance to those who already knew (covenantal aspect) YHWH (cf. Rev. 3:20). Fellowship with YHWH demands an ethical life.

In Amos 5:4 Amos says, "Seek the Lord." This same VERB is also found in Amos 5:14, "seek good and not evil." These three are somewhat parallel. YHWH is said several times to be good (e.g. Ps. 86:5; 100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1,29). Therefore, seeking "Me" and seeking "good" may refer to YHWH (notice the second line of Amos 5:14). This same symbolism can be seen in Hosea 8:2-3.

The Hebrew term "seek" has several meanings.

  1. inquire of
  2. seek a deity in prayer and worship
  3. investigate (to know the heart)
  4. ask or demand

In this context #2 fits best (cf. Deut. 4:29; Hosea 10:12; Isa. 9:13; 31:1; 55:6; 65:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

▣
NASB  "that you may live"
NKJV, NRSV  "and live"
TEV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "and you will live"
NJB  "and you will survive"
REB  "if you would live"

The MT is reflected in NKJV and NRSV. The VERB (BDB 310, KB 309) is a Qal IMPERATIVE parallel to "seek." The sense of the IMPERATIVE is seen in the NASB, TEV, and NJB. Israel's survival as a covenant nation is the issue!

This has always been YHWH's desire (i.e. similar to John 10:10)! YHWH is merciful, if they turn back to Him, He will pardon, restore, and protect (cf. Deut. 30:2-3,10; 32:46,47).

This outburst of mercy is a plea from the heart of YHWH who does not want to destroy His own covenant people (cf. Hosea 11:8-11). They were meant to reveal Him to the nations!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Amos 5:5 "Bethel. . .Gilgal. . .Beersheba"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5 "Bethel. . .Gilgal. . .Beersheba" These are all local centers of worship. The first two were in Israel and the third in southern Judah (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:8; Gen. 21:14, 31; 26:25,33; 46:1) and mentioned earlier in Amos 4:4.

▣ "Beersheba" This was an ancient holy site connected to the Patriarchs (Abraham, Gen. 21:33; Isaac, Gen. 26:23-25; Jacob, Gen. 28:10; 46:1-7) located in southern Judah.

▣ "For Gilgal will certainly go into captivity" Amos is a skilled poet. Here he uses a sound play between "Gilgal" and "to go into exile" (BDB 162, KB 191, a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and a Qal IMPERFECT of the same term, which is a grammatical feature showing intensity). Hebrew poetry is characterized by thought parallelism, multiple meanings of words, and sound plays.

The exact location of Gilgal is unknown. There seem to be at least two mentioned in the OT. See fulll notes at Hosea 9:15 and 12:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "And Bethel will come to trouble" This seems to be a contrast between Bethel (house of God) and what it had become (house of idolatry [aven, BDB 19], cf. Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5,8).

One of the meanings of "trouble" (aven, BDB 19) can be "idolatry" (i.e. "nothing,"cf. Isa. 41:29; 66:3).

entries.title: Amos 5:6 "Seek the Lord that you may live"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:6 "Seek the Lord that you may live" This is parallel to Amos 5:4.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

▣ "He will break forth like a fire" This may be another allusion to Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 4:24). Fire is imagery for the cleansing power of YHWH or to put it another way, His holiness!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

▣ "O house of Joseph" It is unusual for Israel to be called the "house of Joseph" (cf. Amos 6:6). It is usually called the "house of Jacob" (or "house of Israel," e.g. Amos 5:1). However, Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's two children, make up the largest land holdings and the most populous tribes of the northern kingdom.

▣
NASB  "for Bethel"
NKJV  "in Bethel"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "Bethel"
TEV  "the people of Bethel"
NJB  "at Bethel"
LXX, JPSOA footnote  "the House of Israel"
NEB  "Israel"

The MT has "for Bethel" (NASB). The UBS Text Project, p. 283, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt). The NEB follows the LXX, which is a better parallel to "house of Joseph" in the poetic line before. However, it must be admitted that "Bethel" (i.e. "house of God") is mentioned earlier twice in v. 5, but "the house of Israel" also occurs in vv. 1,3.

entries.title: Amos 5:7 "for those who turn justice into wormwood"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7 "for those who turn justice into wormwood" "Justice" is a parallel to "righteousness." These two terms often appear together in the same context in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kgs. 10:9; 1 Chr. 18:14; 2 Chr. 9:8; Ps. 99:4; Isa. 1:21; 5:7; 9:7; 28:17; 32:1,16; 33:5; 59:14; Jer. 4:2; 9:24; 22:3,15; 23:5; 33:15; Ezek. 18:5,19,21,27; 33:14,16,19; 45:9; Amos 5:7,24). This is not the "justification by faith," imputed righteousness of the New Covenant, but the Old Covenant mandate that YHWH wanted a people to fully reveal His character (cf. Matt. 5:19-20,48). However, sinful fallen mankind, even the covenant people, were unable to live out the holiness of God!

The PARTICIPLE (BDB 245, KB 253, Qal PARTICIPLE), when Israel is the subject, is used in a negative sense (cf. Amos 5:7; 6:12; Jer. 2:21). In Amos 4:11 Amos mentioned Sodom and Gomorrah as being overthrown, using the same root but with YHWH as the subject.

Wormwood (BDB 542) refers to any plant that is bitter (cf. UBS's Fauna and Flora of the Bible, p. 198). The rich had prevented justice. The legal system was a bitter thing to the poor, not a haven (cf. Amos 5:12; 6:12). This may be another allusion to idolatry in Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 29:18; Jer. 9:14; 23:15). The cognate in Arabic means "curse."

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣
NASB  "cast righteousness down to the earth"
NKJV  "lay righteousness to rest in the earth"
NRSV  "bring righteousness to the ground"
TEV  "cheat people out of their rights"
NJB, REB  "throw uprightness to the ground"
Peshitta  "lower righteousness to the ground"

The idea here is to cast down (BDB 245, KB 253, Qal PARTICIPLE) with a view toward trampling underfoot (cf. Isaiah 28:2-3). Judges, like the king, were to represent YHWH.

Notice that "justice" and "righteousness" are parallel (cf. Amos 5:24; 6:12). There is an ethical-practical aspect to biblical faith! Biblical faith involves

  1. personal trust
  2. godly living

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

entries.title: Amos 5:8 "the Pleiades"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:8 "the Pleiades" This is literally "heap" or "herd" (BDB 465, KB 472, cf. Job 9:9, 38:31). This was one of the brightest and most popular of the star clusters (Hesiod calls it "the seven sisters") in the constellation Taurus. The UBS, Translator's Handbook, pp. 105, 242, asserts that in Palestine its setting below the horizon introduces winter. This then makes the poetic lines refer to God not as creator only, but active controller (Providence) of the natural order (i.e. Job 9:9).

▣ "Orion" This is literally "fool" (BDB 493, KB 489 II) in the sense of aggressive. It is used to refer to a rebel. The ancients identified this constellation with Nimrod (the warrior, cf. Gen. 10:8-9). It was visible in the summer. God controls the seasons (i.e. the order and regularity of the natural world)! Apparently, God's creation and control of the stars (cf. Gen. 1:14-19) was a necessary theological statement in the light of astral worship (cf. Amos 5:26).

▣ "changes deep darkness into morning" In context this speaks of God's control of the heavenly bodies (cf. Ps. 19: 24). This phrase may be parallel in concept to Amos 4:13c.

▣ "Who calls for the waters of the sea" There are several theories as to the meaning of this phrase:

  1. it refers to the boundaries of the oceans (cf. Gen. 1:9-10)
  2. it refers to YHWH, not Ba'al, as the source of rain (i.e. a blessing to support growth)
  3. it is possibly an allusion to the flood (a judgment motif, cf. Genesis 6)

YHWH controls the waters of creation as He does the stars. Water and the planets are the two things in Genesis 1 that are not said to have been spoken into existence by God (i.e. pre-existing material, cf. Gen. 1:2). See John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One: An Ancient Cosmology.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

▣ "The Lord is His name" The name in Hebrew was very significant in describing the character of an individual. Israel's God's name, "YHWH," is from Exod. 3:14, from the Hebrew VERB "to be."

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

5:9
NASB, REB  "flashes forth"
NKJV  "He rains"
NRSV  "flash out"
TEV, NJB  "brings"

The Hebrew term's (BDB 114, KB 132, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) meaning is in doubt. Its use in Job and the Psalms implies a cheerfulness or joy (meaning of the Arabic root). However, that meaning does not fit Amos at all unless Amos is speaking sarcastically of YHWH smiling at the destruction of idolatrous Israel and her military fortifications. The NASB takes its translation from the possible meaning of the Hiphil, "let something flare up" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 660).

The UBS Text Project, p. 284, gives a textual emendation that turns v. 9 into the names for three constellations (i.e. gods).

  1. bull (BDB 993, KB 1417-1418)
  2. goat (BDB 736, KB 804)
  3. vintager (BDB 130, KB 148)

This forms a parallel with the mentioning of "the Pleiades (i.e. "the cluster") and Orion" (i.e. "the giant") of v. 8.

▣ "the strong" This may refer to the economically and politically powerful (cf. Amos 5:10-13; 2:14). The opposite of "the poor," the very ones who take advantage of them! However, because of the parallel to "fortresses," it may refer to the Israeli military. Also see note above for a connection to constellations.

entries.title: Amos 5:8-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:8-9 This is a poetic doxology to God (Elohim, Gen. 1:1) as Creator and Judge. There are three of these wonderful doxologies in Amos (cf. Amos 4: 4; 5:8-9; 9:5-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

entries.title: Amos 5:10 "They hate him who reproves in the gate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10 "They hate him who reproves in the gate" Those (honest judges, true witnesses) who tried to stand up and defend the poor and helpless (exactly who this refers to is uncertain, some kind of legal advocate) were vehemently attacked by the status quo leadership (cf. Isa. 59:14-15). This is another allusion to Deuteronomy's cursing and blessing section (cf. Deut. 27:25).

The gate was the place of justice in the ancient Near East (cf. Deut. 25:1-3; Ruth 4:1-12). This is where the elders of the communities sat to hear and judicate the issues of the community (cf. Deut. 19:12; 21:3,8,19; 21:3,8; 22:15; 25:7-8). These elders and judges are addressed directly by Amos in vv. 10-17.

For a good brief discussion of Israel's judicial system, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 152-157.

▣ "abhor" This (BDB 1073, KB 1765, Piel IMPERFECT) is a strong VERB, often used to denote YHWH's rejection of idolatry. It is parallel to "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal PERFECT) in this same verse.

▣
NASB  "integrity"
NKJV, Peshitta  "uprightly"
NRSV, NJB  "the truth"
TEV  "the whole truth"
REB  "nothing less than the truth"
JPSOA  "just"

The term's (BDB 1071, KB 1748) basic meaning is to be exact or straight. This imagery for moral/ethical uprightness was derived from the word for a palm tree. Notice its usage.

  1. Noah, Gen. 6:9
  2. Abraham, Gen. 17:1
  3. peace offerings, Lev. 22:21
  4. godly Israelites, Deut. 18:13; Prov. 2:7; 10:9
  5. God, Deut. 32:4 2 Sam. 22:31,33; Ps. 18; 30,32
  6. Job, Job 1:1,8; 2:3
  7. God's word, Ps. 19:7

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLAMELESS, INNOCENT, GUILTLESS, WITHOUT REPROACH, B. 2. b.

entries.title: Amos 5:11a-b
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:11a-b The first two poetic lines of this verse document some of the abuses of the poor:

  1. the options for understanding 11a are
    1. heavy rent (i.e. taken from Akkadian root, NASB, NET, REB, JPSOA)
    2. trample on (i.e. taken from Hebrew root "to trample" [BDB 143, KB 165, Poel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT], cf. NASB (margin), NKJV, NRSV, NJB)
    3. the LXX and Peshitta understand it as a physical blow by the rich to the poor (i.e. possibly imagery for a tax)
  2. a tax on food
  3. bribery at the gate (cf. Amos 5:12)

The term poor (see note at Amos 2:7) may refer to "peasant farmers" (see note at NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 951).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUNGER

entries.title: Amos 5:11c-e
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:11c-e This is another curse for violation of the Mosaic Covenant (cf. Deut. 28:30,39). The rich had built luxurious homes ("well-hewn stone"; also note Amos 3:15) by exploiting the poor (cf. Amos 5:11-12). But YHWH would not let them live with their ill gotten gain (cf. Micah 6:15; Zeph. 1:13). This is an allusion to the Assyrian exile.

entries.title: Amos 5:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:12 This verse, like Amos 5:10-11, lists the sins of the wealthy class against the poor (possibly small farmers) and underprivileged. These are the very ones the ethical God cares about because of their helplessness and vulnerability (cf. Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 16:11; 24:17-22; 26:12-13; 27:19). This is another Deuteronomic emphasis. The prophets always looked back to the Mosaic Covenant (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT]).

The term translated "bribe" (BDB 497 I, KB 495 IV, cf. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 16:19; 27:25; 1 Sam. 12:3; Prov. 6:35) is the same term used to describe God's "covering," "atoning" for sin (KB 493). This important theological term is used here in a derived sense of covering someone's hand or eyes. It is a shocking use of a wonderful theological term.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

entries.title: Amos 5:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:13 This is a very difficult verse because it seems to go against all that the prophet himself advocates and practices. This again may be a play on the semantic field of the PARTICIPLE, "he who is prudent" (BDB 968, KB 1328, Hiphil PARTICIPLE). The Hiphil can mean

  1. look at (to make one wise, cf. Gen. 3:6)
  2. give attention to (e.g. Deut. 32:29)
  3. have comprehension (e.g. Dan. 1:4; 9:25)
  4. give insight, teach (e.g. Dan. 9:22; 11:33,35)
  5. act prudently (e.g. Amos 5:13)
  6. prosper (e.g. Isa. 52:13; Jer. 10:21)
  7. cause to prosper (e.g. Deut. 29:9)

A good example of how this term can mean #5 or #6/#7 see Jer. 23:5. If so the one used here may be another allusion to Deuteronomy (i.e. Deut. 29:9). They were meant to prosper in YHWH's blessing (cf. Deuteronomy 27-29), but they were prospering because they were breaking Moses' Covenant in their treatment of the powerless of their society.

It is also possible (UBS, Handbook, pp. 106-109) to see the key to the structure related to the two people addressed in Amos 5:10.

  1. "they hate. . .they abhor" (v. 10), this group is addressed in Amos 5:11-12
  2. "who reproves. . .who speaks with integrity" (v. 10), these were addressed in Amos 5:13

entries.title: Amos 5:14 "Seek good and not evil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:14 "Seek good and not evil" Note the prophet's sharp contrasts (cf. Amos 5:15). There is a choice to be made which has eternal consequences. "Seek" (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal IMPERATIVE) is another IMPERATIVE. Notice this IMPERATIVE'S relationship with those in Amos 5:4, 6 that emphasize ethical lifestyles. It must be remembered that biblical faith has two foci:

  1. personal relationship (cf. John 3:16; Romans 4)
  2. deeds of love (cf. 1 Corinthians 13; Eph. 2:8-10 and 1 John 3:23)

Amos admonishes Israel to "seek good." Isaiah uses the same VERB to admonish God's people to seek justice (cf. Isa. 1:17). What do we care about, strive for, seek after? The answer to this question tells us who we are and who we serve!

▣ "the Lord God of hosts be with you" This is the greatest promise that God can make (cf. Ps. 23). The title "Lord God of Hosts" has two related meanings in the OT:

  1. YHWH as commander of the angelic army
  2. YHWH as controller of the astral bodies that represent angelic powers (Babylonian idolatry)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

▣ "Just as you have said" Amos may have been referring to

  1. a common teaching of the priests/Levites
  2. an often used liturgy/psalm
  3. the recurrent claim that Israel was the covenant-chosen people (e.g. Exod. 19:5-6; Deut. 7:6; 14:2)

entries.title: Amos 5:15 "Hate evil, love good,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:15 "Hate evil, love good,

 And establish justice in the gate" These are three Hebrew IMPERATIVES:

  1. "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal IMPERATIVE)
  2. "love" (BDB 12, KB 17, Qal IMPERATIVE)
  3. "establish" (BDB 426, KB 427, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)

These reflect the covenant of Moses. Notice that for Amos there is no distinction between the secular and the sacred, between the heart and the hand (cf. Micah 6:8). YHWH's people must reflect YHWH's character!

The command "establish" has the connotation of specific, purposeful action (e.g. Hosea 2:3). YHWH's faithful must determine in their hearts and minds that justice, fairness, and integrity will prevail in their sphere of influence.

▣ "Perhaps the Lord. . .May be gracious to the remnant of Joseph" The prophet is asserting a limited hope (i.e. "perhaps" BDB 19) for those few Israelites who would repent and live out their faith (i.e. "seek Me," Amos 5:4; "seek the Lord," Amos 5:6).

For "remnant" see SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

entries.title: Amos 5:16 "Therefore"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:16 "Therefore" This relates to Amos 5:10-13. It does not relate to the repeated admonition to repent, begun in Amos 5:4-6 (key word, "seek").

▣ "There is wailing in all the plazas. . .'Alas! Alas'" The prophet began the funeral dirge in Amos 5:1; now judgment has come and everybody is wailing.

"Plazas" would be parallel to "gates" or "markets." Even the term "streets" (BDB 299) can mean plaza or market (e.g. 1 Kgs. 20:34).

▣ "farmer" I believe "farmer" is the referent to "the poor." It was not the poor as in modern, western cultures, but the small farmer on ancestral land (given by lot, YHWH, Joshua 12-19) who were being exploited. The Mosaic stipulations of the Sabbath Year and the Jubilee Year were being ignored and land was permanently taken.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II. B., C.

▣ "professional mourners" Near Eastern people are very expressive in their mourning rites. There were trained people available to help in this cultural grieving process (cf. 2 Chr. 35:25; Jer. 9:17). See James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, pp. 283-284.

entries.title: Amos 5:17 "I will pass through the midst of you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:17 "I will pass through the midst of you" This same phrase is used in Exod. 12:12 for the Death Angel passing through Egypt in judgment on the night of Passover. YHWH's coming could be for blessing or judgment (cf. Amos 5:18). Israel viewed it as a certain blessing, but Amos revealed that it would be for judgment. What an ironic, tragic reversal (cf. Amos 5:18-20)! All humans made in God's image sense their need for Him (cf. Amos 5:14b). He wants to be with us, but our actions necessitate judgment, not fellowship!

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEATH ANGEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

entries.title: Amos 5:18 "Alas"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:18 "Alas" This is literally "woe" (BDB 222). This is an interjection of grief and mourning over the dead (cf. Amos 5:16; Jer. 22:18; 34:5). See full note at Amos 6:1.

▣ "you who are longing for the day of the Lord" This VERB (BDB 16, KB 20, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) means "desire for yourselves." These people thought YHWH's coming (i.e. "the day of the Lord") would bring blessings and deliverance because they were covenant people (cf. Amos 3:2). But because of this very reason, judgment would come (cf. Romn. 9:4-5). Because of the blindness of their hearts, YHWH was coming to them as Judge (cf. Amos 3:14; 5:18; 8:3,9,11,13), not Savior (cf. Amos 9:11,13). Their religion resulted in a curse (cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29).

Amos is the first of the writing prophets and this is the first use of the phrase "the Day of the Lord" (see note at Amos 2:16). It is also used often by Joel (cf. Joel 1:15; 2:1,11,31; 3:14). It may have been imagery from the days of "Holy War" (i.e. Joshua and Judges). YHWH was the ever-present provider and protector of His covenant people, but in days of conflict His physical manifestation in miraculous ways delivered His people from danger. However, Israel had so violated the covenant that its privilege had turned to judgment and rejection (cf. Joel 2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "It will be darkness and not light" This continues the contrast on these terms (cf. Amos 4:13c; 5:8c,20).

  1. darkness (BDB 365)
  2. light (BDB 21)

SPECIAL TOPIC: DARKNESS, I.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIGHT

entries.title: Amos 5:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:19 There is absolutely no place to flee from YHWH's judgment (i.e. Job 20:24; Isa. 24:17-18; Jer. 15:2-3).

▣ "lion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Amos 5:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:20 What irony! What tragedy!

▣ "with no brightness in it" The "brightness" (BDB 618 I, KB 667 I ) may be an allusion to the glory of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

entries.title: Amos 5:21 "I hate, I reject your festivals,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:21 "I hate, I reject your festivals,

 Nor do I delight in your solemn assemblies" These are strong terms! They were very religious (i.e. Amos 4:4-5), but their attitudes and hearts were far from God (cf. Isa. 6:9-10. Their religiosity was an abomination to God (cf. Isa. 29:13)! The first two VERBS, "I hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338) and "I reject" (BDB 549, KB 540) are Qal PERFECTS, which denote a settled, complete attitude.

The term "festivals" (BDB 290, KB 290) is often used to denote the three major annual feasts (cf. Exod. 23:15-16; Lev. 23). These were required feasts for all males.

The term "delight" (BDB 926, KB 1280, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is literally "smell," which refers to the Mosaic phrase "soothing aroma," denoting YHWH's acceptance of a sacrifice (e.g. Gen. 8:21; Exod. 29:18,25; Lev. 26:31; 1 Sam. 26:19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, I. D. #1-3

SPECIAL TOPIC: A SOOTHING AROMA

entries.title: Amos 5:21-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:21-24 Do these verses show that YHWH rejects the sacrificial system given in Leviticus 1-7? There are many strong passages in the Prophets that show YHWH's displeasure at His people's practice of the sacrificial system (cf. Isa. 1:11-17; Jer. 6:20; 7:21-23; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-27; Micah 6:6-8). The sacrificial system was YHWH's way of dealing with human sin so as to develop and continue a personal, loving, trusting relationship with His highest creation. The problem was not the Mosaic Covenant and sacrifice, but human abuses of it. However, Israel not only turned it into mere ritual and form, but even merged it with pagan practices.

  1. YHWH wants fellowship!
  2. YHWH wants a people who reflect His character!
  3. YHWH wants to reach all humans through the witness of a chosen group (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Amos 5:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:22 Religiosity without relationship is an abomination (cf. Amos 4:4-5; Isa. 1: 10-20; Jer. 7). YHWH does not reject the sacrificial system, but its inappropriate use (ritual without repentant faith; form without appropriate attitude and lifestyle action)!

▣ "I will not even look" "Look" (BDB 613, KB 661, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is used in the sense of accept or acknowledge.

▣ "fatlings" This (BDB 597, KB 635) refers to specially cared for young animals which were raised to be sacrificed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURNT OFFERINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRAIN OFFERINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE OFFERINGS

entries.title: Amos 5:23 "take away from Me the noise of your songs"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:23 "take away from Me the noise of your songs" This (BDB 693, KB 747) is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE MASCULINE SINGULAR. Even sacred, glorious music without the proper motive is a farce, hypocrisy, and an abomination to God. God desires faith, not only form!

This verse does show that the northern tribes adopted the worship forms (i.e. music by the guilds, cf. 1 Sam. 10:5) of the temple in Jerusalem (developed by David, cf. 2 Sam. 6:5,15). The leaders (Jeroboam I) wanted these northern altars (i.e. Dan and Bethel) to duplicate the worship techniques so that the common people would not sense a difference.

It is surprising that the VERBS are SINGULAR. It is just possible that in Amos 5:23 Amos is addressing the high priest at Bethel.

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, NIV, Peshitta  "harps"
NKJV, NET  "stringed instruments"
NJB  "lyres"
REV, JPSOA  "lutes"
LXX  "instruments"

As the number of English translations demonstrates, moderns do not know to what type of stringed instrument this refers (BDB 614, KB 664 II). To note the number of other instruments it is often associated with see 2 Sam. 6:5 and Ps. 92:3. It is possible that Assyrian wall pictures have depicted this instrument as strings with a sounding box, something like our bass fiddle. See James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible pp. 221-222.

entries.title: Amos 5:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:24 This is one of the most famous verses in Amos. YHWH desires His people to focus on who He is, not on certain worship days, but on every day. True faith is what we are, not what we do; but who we are will be clearly seen in what we do, how we do it, and why we do it (cf. Matt. 7; Eph. 1:4; 2:10).

"Justice" and "righteousness" are parallel, as in Amos 5:7. In this context they refer to human obedience to the Mosaic Covenant lived out in a proper relationship between God and godly living.

The VERB "roll down" (BDB 146, KB 193) is a Niphal JUSSIVE, which denotes an IMPERATIVE sense.

▣ "an ever-flowing stream" This (BDB 450, KB 44) refers to a spring that never runs dry (i.e. is not seasonal). It is a powerful imagery for a life of active faith (cf. Jer. 22:3; Ezek. 45:9; Micah 6:8).

entries.title: Amos 5:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:25 This is a very difficult verse to interpret. It can be a question or an affirmation (cf. TEV). There have been two lines of interpretation:

  1. Amos is asserting that the children of Israel did not sacrifice in the wilderness (cf. Jer. 7:21-22 and NJB)
  2. although they did sacrifice in a limited (JB) way, the object of their sacrifice was not YHWH, but Assyrian gods who were leading them (sarcasm) into exile.

entries.title: Amos 5:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:26 There is much discussion on the time element of this verse. Does it refer to the forty years of wilderness wandering of Amos 5:25 or does it refer to the future wanderings of the Assyrian exile? It seems that because the idols mentioned are Assyrian star gods (i.e. Akkadian names for Saturn) this verse is referring to current time, while Amos 5:25 refers to the wilderness wanderings after the Exodus from Egypt.

Another possibility is that Israel had made the sacrificial system ultimate when in fact they could not perform it after they left Egypt for many years (no tabernacle). During those years personal trust in God's care, presence, and provision was the focus of their faith, not sacrifice. This does not depreciate the sacrificial system. It was surely the will of God, but God Himself was the goal, not the ritual, liturgy, and cultus! Motive and attitude were crucial!

Just a note about Stephen's quote of Amos 5:25-27 in Acts 7:42-43. Most Jews of the first century A.D. used the Septuagint translation of the OT. In some places it follows a different Hebrew text from the Masoretic Text. This is a problem! However, even in the Dead Sea Scrolls both traditions are present. None of the verses affect the truth or trustworthiness of doctrine or practice. We must realize that Christianity does not stand or fall on difference between the Hebrew OT and its ancient versions or NT manuscript variation. See a discussion of this in Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp 381-382.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

▣ "Sikkuth your king" The MT has "Sakkuth" (BDB 696, KB 753), meaning uncertain because apparently Jewish scribes substituted vowels from derogatory terms. The LXX has "booth of" or "tabernacle of," however, this term is found in Assyrian documents to refer to a war god named Adar-Melek, which refers to Saturn (Ninurta in Ugaritic). Notice a deity is called "king," which shows the cultural background for YHWH as king.

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "Kiyyun"
NKJV, Pehsitta  "Chiun"
NRSV, TEV, NJB  "Kaiwan"
NIV, REB  "the pedestal"
LXX  "Raiphan"

This also refers to an Assyrian star god, who is also identified with the planet Saturn (BDB 475). The NASB reflects the Hebrew spelling which is a combination of the consonants of the name of the star god, but the vowels from the Hebrew word "abominations" (BDB 1055, JPSOA footnote). This was a common way for Hebrew scribes to ridicule the names of gods, kings, and nations (e.g. Sikkuth).

The spelling "Kaiwan" is from Akkadian or Arabic root.

The translation of the term as "pedestal" supposes that the term comes from the root, "to be firm" (kwn).

The JPSOA suggests that vv. 26-27 would fit well after Amos 6:14.

entries.title: Amos 5:27 "I will make you go into exile beyond Damascus"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:27 "I will make you go into exile beyond Damascus" This refers to the Assyrian exile, which occurred in 722 B.C. after a three year siege of Samaria (cf. possibly Amos 4:3; and Hosea 9:3; 10:6; 11:5). This again is an allusion to the cursings and blessings section of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29.

▣ "says the Lord, whose name is God of hosts" One of the names for Israel's God is "YHWH of hosts" or "YHWH Sabaoth" (cf. 1 Sam. 1:3). In this text Elohim is substituted for YHWH (cf. Ps. 80:7,14,19). Here, the title is connected to God as the controller of a heavenly army (i.e. the stars). YHWH, not astral deities (i.e. Assyrian star gods), was Israel's hope!

The worship of the lights of the sky is condemned in many texts (cf. Deut. 4:19; 8:2; 17:2-5; 2 Kgs. 23:4-5,11; Jer. 8:2; 19:13; 32:29; Zeph. 1:5). The OT asserts several times that God created and controls the heavenly lights (cf. Gen. 1:14-19; Ps. 19:1-6; Neh. 9:6). It is in connection with these texts that "Lord of hosts" is a condemnation of idolatry (the worship of gods/angels/spirits of the heavenly lights, cf. LXX of Deut. 32:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Amos 6:1 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:1 "Woe" The pronunciation of His Hebrew word sounds like exasperated or sorrowful feelings. This term (BDB 222) characterizes the book of Lamentations. The Prophets often used the literary form (a 3-2 beat) of a funeral dirge to express the disapproval of God and His coming judgment. This term is recurrent in Isaiah.

  1. negative in Isa. 1:4,24; 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; 10:1; 17:12; 18:1; 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1; 45:9,10
  2. neutral in Isa. 10:5
  3. positive in Isa. 55:1, and Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 22:13,18; 23:1; 30:7; 34:5; 47:6; 48:1; 50:27)

This INTERJECTION is followed by a series of PARTICIPLES, which carries the "woe" thought with each of them (Amos 6:1-7).

▣ "to those who are at ease" There is no VERB. This phrase is used as a SUBSTANTIVE. It has the prophetic connotation of "careless, wanton, arrogant" (BDB 983, KB 1375, cf. Isa. 32:9,11; Zech. 1:15; and Ps. 123:4). It was not their leisure or wealth or social status that was the problem, but their trust in these things instead of God.

The group is characterized in several ways in the next few verses:

  1. those who feel secure, Amos 6:1b
  2. you who put away the evil day, Amos 6:3
  3. those who lie on beds of ivory, Amos 6:4
  4. those who improvise (sing idle songs), Amos 6:5
  5. those who drink wine from sacrificial bowls, Amos 6:6

All of these phrases have the DEFINITE ARTICLE plus a PARTICIPLE.

▣ "in Zion" This seems to be parallel to "in the mountain of Samaria" (the capital of the Northern Ten Tribes). However, Zion is one of the seven hills of Jerusalem. Therefore, this could mean

  1. covenant people as a whole, Amos 3:1; 6:8
  2. Judah and Israel were both sinful and guilty
  3. a literary parallel, but with no distinction intended
  4. The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA, p. 1187 footnote d) suggests a possible emendation, "to Zion," which is "Joseph," which would parallel "hill of Samaria" better. Joseph is referred to in Amos 6:6, and in Amos 5:6,15 it was a way to refer to the northern tribes.
  5. Both the Peshitta and LXX translate it as referring to Israel's opposition to Judah.
    1. LXX ‒ "set at naught Zion"
    2. Peshitta ‒ "despise Zion"

SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION

▣
NASB  "the distinguished men"
NKJV  "notable persons"
NRSV, NJB, JPSOA  "the notables"
REB  "men of mark"
TEV  "you great leaders"
Peshitta  "the chiefs"
LXX  "the heads"

The MT is literally "pierced men" (BDB 666, #2; KB, 718, Qal PARTICIPLE), which makes no sense here. An Arabic root means "one who scrutinizes" (i.e. leaders). This seems to refer to

  1. former leaders from the surrounding nations, with whom Israel was trying to make security agreements to protect themselves from the judgment of YHWH (i.e. Assyrian exile)
  2. what these wealthy leaders thought of themselves (cf. Amos 6:13; NET Bible; Tyndale Commentary)

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Amos 6:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:2  Depending on how one interprets Amos 6:1, this verse would be

  1. Amos' words to the arrogant leadership of the covenant people (Judah and Israel) similar to Amos 9:7. However, this involved some textual emendations (cf. UBS, Handbook, #31, p. 289)
  2. the leaders' comments to the people (cf. NET Bible, Tyndale commentary)

▣ "Calneh" This was a fortified city in Syria (BDB 484, cf. Isa. 10:9), which was destroyed by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 B.C. It became a proverb of the coming exile of Israel (cf. Isa. 10:9-11). It was on this occasion that the king of Israel, Menahen, began to give tribute to Assyria.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA, #19

▣ "Hamath" The Anchor Bible Dictionary, vol. 3, p. 33, has a good brief comment.

"A city in Syria, the southern border of which often became part of the formula for the northern idealized border of Israel (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:65; 1 Chr. 13:5). The city was an object of the Assyrian conquest (Isa. 36:19), and some of its inhabitants were exiled and settled in Israel (2 Kgs. 17:24)."

It (BDB 333) was located about 150 miles north of the city of Dan on the Orantes River.

▣ "Gath" The Philistines established five city-states in southwest Judah on the coastal plain. Four of those cities are mentioned earlier in Amos 1:6-8, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron). Gath (BDB 387 III) was captured by David in 1 Chronicles 18 and is also mentioned in Micah 1:10. It was later destroyed by the Assyrians.

▣ "Or is their territory greater than yours?" The JPSOA suggests an emendation that reverses this phrase, "Or is your territory larger than theirs," p. 1187 footnote, "f." The UBS Text Project, p. 287, suggests the translation, "if small states like Kalneh, Hamath, Gath are flourishing, how much more this will be the case with the greater States of Judah and Israel!" It also suggests an interpretation, "This discourse reflects the blind self-confidence of those who speak in this manner."

SPECIAL TOPIC: PHILISTINES

entries.title: Amos 6:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3 The wealthy leaders were "putting off" (BDB 622, KB 672, Piel PARTICIPLE; this VERB appears only here in this form and only twice in the OT (cf. Isa. 66:5) the day of YHWH's visitation by

  1. divination (SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION)
  2. trying to ignore (cf. TEV) the covenant consequences of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29

The irony is that by their very acts they were hastening the day!

▣ "the seat of violence" This could refer to

  1. the leaders of Israel
  2. the coming invasion of Assyria

"Seat" (BDB 443) is understood as "throne," which is imagery for "reign."

entries.title: Amos 6:4 "sprawl"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:4 "sprawl" The term (BDB 710, KB 769, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE) is used again in Amos 6:7. It has a negative connotation. It is parallel to "recline" (BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal PARTICIPLE), which may have been an unusual way to eat at this time in Palestine. If so, then both denote new, foreign, and non-traditional actions (i.e. pagan influence on Israeli leaders).

entries.title: Amos 6:4-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:4-6 This describes the elaborate drunken banquets of the self-indulgent rich of the northern tribes (i.e. Joseph in line 3 of v. 6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

entries.title: Amos 6:5 "Who improvise"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:5 "Who improvise" The VERB "improvise" (BDB 827, KB 967, Qal PARTICIPLE) is uncertain in meaning. It appears only here in the OT. In later Hebrew it means "break off" or "divide" (e.g. fruit that drops off the tree or bush). The translation "compose" or "improvise" comes from the Arabic root.

JPSOA suggests "they hum snatches of song."

It is just possible in this context that these revelers are desecrating

  1. David's melodies, poems used in temple worship
  2. the instruments used in the temple (LXX)

▣ "like David have composed songs" This is a historical allusion to David's musical background.

  1. David himself
    1. played for Saul, 1 Sam. 16:16,23; 18:10; 19:9
    2. appointed Levitical singers, 1 Chr. 6:31; 15:1-16:43; 25:1-31; 2 Chr. 29:25-30
    3. designed or used musical instruments in his songs, Neh. 12:36; 1 Chr. 23:5
  2. examples of David's music
    1. 2 Samuel 22
    2. most of first two books of Psalm (cf. Ps. 72:72)
      (1) MT asserts 73 psalms
      (2) LXX asserts 84 psalms
      (3) Vulgate asserts 53 psalms
  3. called "the sweet psalmist of Israel" (cf. 2 Sam. 23:1)
▣
NASB  "have composed songs for themselves"
NKJV, NJB, REB, NET  "invent for themselves musical
  instruments"
NRSV  "improvise on instruments of music"
JPSOA  "account themselves musicians"
Peshitta  "consider themselves skilled in the
  musical instruments"
LXX  "who excel in the sound of
  musical instruments"

The MT VERB (BDB 363, KB 359, Qal PERFECT) usually means "to think" or "to account," but BDB #1,5 suggest "invent" (NKJV, NJB, REB) in this context.

6:6
NASB  "sacrificial bowls"
NKJV, NRSV  "bowls"
TEV, NJB, REB  "by the bowl full"
LXX  "through filtered wine"
Peshitta  "pure wine"

This is not so much an expression of the sacrilegious use (cf. Dan. 5:2) of sacred utensils (cf. Exod. 24:6-8; Num. 7:13) as it is an expression of their drunkenness ("bowls, not cups"; TEV, NJB, REB, "you drink wine by the bowlful"). Some see this as a magical practice based on Isa. 65:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "they anoint themselves with the finest of oils" Putting oil on one's face and arms was a sign of gladness. Their actions are in contrast to the next line of poetry. They should have been grieving over the ruin of their nation.

The VERB has a wide semantical field but is not used elsewhere in the OT for festival anointing. In this context, it may take on another example of inappropriate use of a ceremonial practice (i.e. covenant violation).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the ruin of Joseph" Joseph married an Egyptian. They had two children who were adopted by Jacob (Israel, cf. Gen. 48:8-22). Although the Messianic line came through Judah, Joseph received the "double inheritance" of the oldest child. Joseph's two sons became the two largest tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. They were part of the ten northern tribes who broke away from Solomon's son, Rehoboam, in 922 B.C. and started a new state under Jeroboam I. This new state was known by several titles:

  1. Israel (Jacob's new name)
  2. Samaria (capital)
  3. Ephraim (largest tribe)

entries.title: Amos 6:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:7 This refers to YHWH's judgment on these who cared only for themselves, but claimed to know God (i.e. the northern kingdom)! Their judgment is the exact reversal of their lifestyles! First in extravagance and revelry; first in exile!

▣ "banqueting" This term (BDB 931, KB 634) is found only twice in the OT (here and Jer. 16:5). The Jeremiah text (and one Ugaritic text) links this term with a self-indulgent pagan feast for the dead! If so, the sarcasm of Amos' statement is obvious.

It is another example of Israel abusing YHWH's law by adopting pagan rites or flaunting Mosaic regulations.

entries.title: Amos 6:8-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:8-11 The UBS, Handbook for Translators, p. 131, makes a good point that these verses parallel Amos 5:21-24. With God's wrath (cf. Amos 6:8; 5:24) comes God's devastating, complete judgment!

entries.title: Amos 6:8 "The Lord God has sworn by Himself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:8 "The Lord God has sworn by Himself" For "the Lord God" (i.e. Adon YHWH), see note at Amos 4:2.

The VERB "swear" (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT) is used several times in Amos referring to YHWH swearing

  1. by His holiness, Amos 4:2
  2. by Himself, Amos 6:8
  3. by the pride of Jacob, Amos 8:7 (sarcasm, irony, or regret)

▣ "the Lord God of hosts" The repetition of these two names for Israel's Deity makes this an emphasized pronouncement.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "I loathe the arrogance of Jacob" The VERB (BDB 1060 II, KB 1672, Piel PARTICIPLE) is a rare (only here in the OT) but a powerful term of rejection (see all the versions). BDB has "loathe," KB has "to make repulsive, desecrate." It is parallel to "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338, cf. Amos 5:21).

The term "arrogance" (BDB 144) means "exaltation," "majesty," or "excellence." It is used in a positive sense toward Israel in Ps. 47:4. In this context it refers to Amos 6:4-6. See sarcastic parallel in Amos 8:7. Israel's inappropriate "pride" receives God's judgment (cf. Hosea 5:5; 7:10)!

entries.title: Amos 6:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:9-10 This is prose, not poetry.

entries.title: Amos 6:9 "ten men"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:9 "ten men" This number was important to the Jews because it was the minimum number required for worship (in Babylon during the exile ten men were required to start a synagogue) and other social events, possibly even military groups. Because of the use of the number ten, this judgment verse may relate to Amos 5:3.

entries.title: Amos 6:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:10 This verse seems to describe the siege of Samaria, the capital of Israel. There will be so many people dead and the plague so rampant that bodies will be burned indiscriminately (cf. Amos 8:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CREMATION

▣ "one's uncle, or his undertaker" There are many questions about this phrase.

  1. Are there two people or one?
  2. What does the word (BDB 976) translated "undertaker" by the NASB, but literally means "he who burns," mean?

For question #1 the phrase refers to two different people who talk together in the rest of the verse (i.e. so there is no survivor in the recesses of the house).

For question #2 there have been many theories:

  1. one who burns deceased bodies
  2. embalming or anointing the dead with spices
  3. one who burns incense on behalf of the dead
  4. one who burns a sacrifice on behalf of the dead
  5. a parallel term for a near relative. The first term would mean a near kin on the mother's side and the second term a near kin on the father's side.

For me #1 or #5 seems best. But #4 could be linked to the banquet for the dead in Amos 6:6.

▣ "Keep quiet. For the name of the Lord is not to be mentioned" This is a theological affirmation of who sent the invasion. The aftermath of judgment causes a holy reverence for YHWH, missing so long in Israel.

The phrase "keep quiet" (BDB 245, a Hebrew INTERJECTION) is used in contexts of YHWH's presence (cf. Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13) and judgment (cf. Amos 8:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH, D.

entries.title: Amos 6:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:11 This is the concluding point of Amos 6:8-11. Judgment (by a foreign nation, i.e. Assyria) will fall on great and small (i.e. all the population). No one will escape (cf. Amos 5:18-20).

▣ "to pieces. . .to fragments" The first term's (BDB 944, KB 1249) meaning is uncertain:

  1. used of rain droplets (Song of Songs 5:2)
  2. chopped food
  3. to shatter or grind

The second term (BDB 132, KB 149) means to break open (cf. Ps. 141:7), like a wall (cf. Isa. 22:9). The VERB form implies a tearing into pieces (Piel). David Allan Hubbard, Joel and Amos (Tyndale OT Commentaries), asserts that these two terms fit an earthquake better than an invasion. He also lists the other places in Amos where he thinks the texts fit an earthquake (cf. Amos 1:1; 2:13; 8:8; 9:1-6), p.198.

entries.title: Amos 6:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:12 These first two questions are somewhat difficult in Hebrew, but it is obvious they refer to unnatural acts. All these rhetorical questions expect a "no" answer. It was also unnatural for God's people to turn justice into poison!

▣ "Do horses run on rocks" "Rocks" (BDB 700, KB 758) refers to large boulders or possibly to horses running up cliffs or over crags. The answer is obviously "no."

▣ "does one plow them with oxen" It is possible to change the MT's vowels and dividing of consonants to read "plow the sea" (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET, JPSOA footnote). This is accomplished by taking the PLURAL ending of "oxen" as a separate word, "sea." This fits the context better. As v. 12a, it is meant to be an impossible act. All four questions expect a "no" answer!

The UBS Text Project, p. 289, gives "with oxen" a "B" rating (some doubt). It assumes that line 2 refers to "plowing a rock with oxen."

▣ "justice. . .fruit of righteousness" See note at Amos 5:12.

entries.title: Amos 6:13 "You who rejoice"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:13 "You who rejoice" This Hebrew phrase implies arrogance and pride over two military victories by Jeroboam II of the trans-Jordan cities of Lodebar and Karnaim. Israel was proud and confident in her military, but YHWH will destroy Israel by a greater military power (cf. Amos 6:14, the Assyrians)! The Assyrians will come from the same geographical direction as these two cities mentioned, "the north."

▣
NASB, TEV, JPSOA  "Lodebar"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB  "Lo Debar"
Rotherham, NRSV footnote, REB, Peshitta  "in a thing of nothing"

The MT apparently has the name of a city (BDB 520, cf. 2 Sam. 9:4,5;17:27) but the UBS Text Project, p. 289, gives "for nothing" an "A" rating (almost certain).

However, in context, Lodebar seems to be parallel to the city of "Karnaim" (BDB 902).

  1. MT ‒ "in Lo-debar" ‒ ל לא דבר
  2. Peshitta ‒ ללא דבר

▣ "Have we not by our own strength taken Karnaim for ourselves" This is apparently another city in the trans-jordan area. The term (BDB 902) means "a pair of horns," which would denote its power. These cities were both recaptured by Jeroboam II (782-753 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 14:25).

The theological implication of the phrase is that Israel, by her own military power, captured these two cities, which goes against the concept of holy war. It was YHWH's power and strength (e.g. Exod. 13:3,14,16) that enabled His people to win in battle. This claim is another sign of Israel's arrogance and covenant ignorance.

entries.title: Amos 6:14 "I am going to raise up a nation against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:14 "I am going to raise up a nation against you" This refers to Assyria (cf. Isa. 10:5).

▣ "the Lord God of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Arabah" This is the traditional boundary of the Promised Land (cf. Num. 34:7-8; Josh. 13:5; Jdg. 3:3; 1 Kgs. 8:65; 2 Kgs. 14:25). Judah would also be affected!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why did God reject the sacrifices of the northern tribes?
  2. Why is God's creative act emphasized? (Amos 6:8-9)
  3. Why is Amos 5:25-26 so difficult to interpret?
  4. Is Amos condemning wealth and the sacrificial system or something else? What?

entries.title: Amos 7:1 "Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:1 "Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold" This introduction shows the relatedness of the visions (cf. Amos 7:1,4,7; 8:1, but not 9:1-10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "He was forming" These visions and judgments were from YHWH Himself (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal PARTICIPLE, MASCULINE SINGULAR).

▣ "a locust-swarm" This type of plague is mentioned in Exod. 10:12ff. It was specifically one of the curses mentioned in Deut. 28:38-42, if YHWH's people did not keep his commandments.

There are over twelve different words in the Hebrew language translated "locusts," which show the fear and commonness of this plague. It is uncertain if these words refer to types of locust or stages of their growth (see my exegetical notes on Joel 1:4; 2:25). See UBS, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 53-54. This is a helpful resource!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "the spring crop began to sprout" This is literally "the latter growth" (BDB 545, KB 536). It is uncertain if this refers to grass or grain. It is also uncertain if it is a second growth or a replanting. This would have been sometime after April. The later rain had to occur before the seeds would sprout. If this crop was lost there would be no crop until the next year!

▣ "after the king's mowing" This is literally "shearings" (BDB 159, KB 186). This phrase is not meant to teach that the king received the first mowing as a tax on the land. This allotment for the king is mentioned only here in the entire OT. The phrase was meant to be a way to date this event in the spring.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Amos 7-9 forms the last literary unit. The book can be broken into three divisions: (1) judgments against the nations; (2) judgments against Judah and Israel; and (3) the visions of Amos.
    1. The visions of Amos can be outlined.:
      1. Amos 7, three visions
      2. Amos 8, one vision
      3. Amos 9, one vision.
    2. Judgment Visions
      1. Locust, Amos 7:1-3
      2. Fire (possibly famine, cf. Amos 4:6-8; 8:11-13), 7:4-6
      3. Plumb line (possibly weak fortifications), Amos 7:7-9
      4. Summer fruit, Amos 8:1-3
      5. Earthquake, Amos 9:1-2 (also possibly Amos 8:7-10)
    3. It is surely possible that these visions were the very means of God's prophetic call to Amos from shepherd to prophet. The prophet calls for mercy (visions 1 & 2), but the reality of rebellion, idolatry, and unrepentance demanded judgment. Israel must be told so they will know it is not YHWH's weakness or lack of compassion, but their sin that has brought this on them (also a warning to Judah).

  2. Amos 7:10-17 is unique because
    1. it gives biographical information about Amos (notice how many of the visions are related to agriculture)
    2. it is written in the THIRD PERSON while other sections of the book are in the FIRST PERSON (i.e. evidence of a compiler or later editor)

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Amos 7:2 "finished"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:2 "finished" This VERB (BDB 477, KB 476, Piel PERFECT) has the connotation of "to complete" or "destroy" (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 641). Here it functions in both senses.

▣ "that I said" The Prophets often serve as intercessors (cf. Exod. 32:11; Jer. 15:1; 18:20; Ezek. 9:8; Dan. 9:15-19), although usually they speak to the covenant people on YHWH's behalf.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

▣ "Lord God" This is Adon and YHWH, used so often in Amos (cf. Jer. 14:7,20,21; Ezek. 9:8; 11:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "please pardon" This (BDB 669, KB 757) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. This word is always used for YHWH's forgiveness of humans (see Robert B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 135-136).

Amos, the prophet of social justice, has become the intercessor for mercy! The hammer of the message of judgment has mellowed at the consequences of judgment!

It is noteworthy that Amos asked YHWH to pardon. One wonders if this means

  1. let the judgment pass
  2. forgive their sin so there is no need for judgment

Amos makes this same request for the first two visions. However Amos meant the prayer, YHWH took it in sense #1. When the third and fourth visions come there is no mercy because there has been no repentance! The time of respite was not used for spiritual renewal, but further rebellion. Patience and mercy have turned into wrath (cf. Amos 7:8,9; 8:7,10,11)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORGIVENESS IN THE OT

entries.title: Amos 7:2,5 "Jacob. . .For he is small"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:2,5 "Jacob. . .For he is small" Notice that the prophet's appeal is to the nation's "need" not to their "covenant relationship." The Lord had promised that Abraham's seed would be as

  1. the stars of heaven (e.g. Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4)
  2. the sand of the seashore (e.g. Gen. 22:17; 32:12)
  3. the dust of the earth (e.g. Gen. 13:16; 28:14; Num. 23:10)

but now there were so few!

7:3
NASB, TEV  "The Lord changed His mind
  about this"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA  "The Lord relented
  concerning this"
LXX  "Repent, O Lord at this"
Peshitta  "averted this calamity"

This Arabic root means "to breathe heavy" (BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal PERFECT). This is anthropomorphic imagery for divine repentance. The root of this word expresses deep feelings (see Robert B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 87-88). The prophet Nahum carries this term in his name.

YHWH is often spoken of in the Bible in two ways.

  1. as changing His mind or relenting (cf. Ps. 106:45; Jer. 18:8; 26:3,13,19; Amos 7:3,6; Joel 2:13-14; Jonah 3:10; 4:2)
  2. not changing (cf. 1 Sam. 15:29; Jer. 4:28; Zech. 8:14)

He is affected by

  1. our prayers
  2. His unchanging character of compassion and love (cf. Exod. 3:7; Jdg. 2:18; Hosea 11:8-9; Joel 2:13-14; Amos 5:15)

However, this should not be understood in the sense that His nature or purpose vacillates. It does not change (cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; Mal. 3:6; Heb. 13:8; James 1:17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

7:4
NASB  "contend"
NKJV  "conflict"
NRSV (footnote), Peshitta  "a judgment"
TEV  "preparing to punich"
NJB, REB, JPSOA  "summoning"
LXX  "called for a sentence"

This term (BDB 936, KB 1224) in this context, refers to a legal case against Israel (i.e. a divorce case, e.g. Hosea 4:1; 12:2; Micah 6:1-2) and its consequences.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVORCE

▣
MT, NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, Peshitta, LXX  "by fire"
NRSV, NET  "a shower of fire"
TEV  "with fire"
REB, JPSOA (footnote)  "flaming fire"
NJB  "fire"

Fire (BDB 77, #5) is often used as a symbol of judgment (e.g. Amos 2:5; Deut. 32:22; Isa. 66:15-16). In this agricultural context the fire may refer to the scorching heat of the sun or the plants being defoliated by the locusts. If so, "the great deep" may be a reference to available water (i.e. springs, rivers, rain, etc., cf. Amos 1:2; 4:6-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

SPECIAL TOPIC: EAST WIND

▣ "the great deep" This refers to the underground water source of rivers (cf. Gen. 1:2; 7:11; 49:15; Ps. 36:6; Isa. 51:10). This is a mythological term from the earliest known Mesopotamian nations, Sumer and Babylon, but in the OT it has been totally stripped of its mythological connotation. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter 13, "The Language of Myth," pp. 219-242.

In this context it refers to God's allowing foreign invaders to destroy Israel.

entries.title: Amos 7:5 "please stop"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:5 "please stop" This (BDB 292, KB 292) is another Qal IMPERATIVE with waw. However, notice this time the prophet did not appeal for forgiveness, but for the cessation of judgment. YHWH is merciful, but there is an end to His patience (cf. Amos 7:8; 8:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Amos 7:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:6 See full exegetical note at Amos 7:3.

entries.title: Amos 7:7 "the Lord was standing by a vertical wall"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:7 "the Lord was standing by a vertical wall" This seems to imply a wall of loose stones removed from the fields. With time these stones shifted their positions and became unstable and unsafe.

▣ "a plumb line" This is the only use of this particular term (BDB 59, KB 71) in the OT. It was a construction tool (cord with metal weight at the end) used to test the perpendicular alignment of buildings or walls. It is used figuratively here to express judgment because mankind has deviated from the standard of God (cf. 2 Kgs. 21:13; Isa. 28:17; 34:11; Lam. 2:8).

Although most English translations (NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB) accept "plumb line" as the implied contextual meaning, it is possible to argue for "tin" (NET) as the proper translation of this Akkadian loan word. The UBS Text Project, p. 292, gives "on a wall of tin" an "A" rating. If so, then the imagery would be that of a tin wall, thereby, imagery for "apparent protection" (i.e. a wall of weak metal, tin). Several prophets used metal imagery (cf. Jer. 15:20; Ezek. 4:3).

Whichever it is, this is a vision of judgment (i.e. possibly "grief," similar post biblical root, NET Bible footnote). Israel thinks she is militarily secure and spiritually orthodox, but she is not!

entries.title: Amos 7:8 "I will spare them no longer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:8 "I will spare them no longer" Literally "I will never (BDB 414, KB 418, Hiphil IMPERFECT) again pass by (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal INFINITIVE) them." Amos realizes the depth of Israel's rebellion and ceases to intercede on her behalf.

entries.title: Amos 7:9 "high places. . .sanctuaries"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:9 "high places. . .sanctuaries" The "high places" (BDB 119, cf. Jer. 7:31; 19:5) refer to the local fertility worship sites ("will be desolated," BDB 1030, KB 1053, Niphal PERFECT with waw, cf. Hosea 10:8), while "the sanctuaries" (BDB 874) refer to the national shrines ("will be laid waste," BDB 351, KB 349, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) at the cities of Dan and Bethel, started by Jeroboam I (922 B.C.)

Because of Isa. 16:12, these two terms may refer to the same worship site (possibly "open air," not a building).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "the house of Jeroboam" This refers to Jeroboam I, who led the rebellion of the Northern Ten Tribes in 922 B.C. against Solomon's son, Rehoboam, over the issue of forced labor and heavy taxation. The true issue was his setting up alternate temples at Bethel and Dan (i.e. the two golden calves).

For a good discussion on "forced labor," see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 141-142.

▣ "the sword" The sword (i.e. war) is to be paralleled with the severity of the locust swarm of Amos 7:1. and the consuming fire of Amos 7:4.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

entries.title: Amos 7:10 "Amaziah the priest"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:10 "Amaziah the priest" This was the chief priest (i.e. from the Aramaic Targums) of the national golden calf shrine at Bethel. Here we see the dilemma of the people when confronted by two representatives of YHWH. The Priest and the Prophet both claim to speak for God, both claim to have His authority.

▣ "Jeroboam" This refers to Jeroboam II (cf. Amos 1:1), the current king of Israel. As is often the case the exact dates of his reign vary from scholar to scholar:

  1. John Bright, 786-746 B.C.
  2. E. J. Young, 783-743 B.C.
  3. R. K. Harrison, 782/81-753 B.C.

There are several problems connected to dating OT events:

  1. the only clear link between secular history and the OT is the battle of Charchemish in 605 B.C.
  2. the reigns of the kings overlap (co-reigns)
  3. the Babylonians and Palestinians date the reign of their kings differently (i.e. count or do not count first partial year)

See Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings.

▣ "Amos has conspired against you" Amaziah accused Amos of political treason ("conspired," BDB 905, KB 1153, Qal PERFECT, for examples of the use of this term see 2 Sam. 15:12; 2 Kgs. 11:14; 15:15). Near Eastern kings were very conscious of their prophet's words and popularity among the populace and feared any negative prediction (e.g. Herod Antipas and John the Baptist).

▣ "the land is unable to endure all his words" Amos is speaking at Bethel. All the geographical directions of the book are given from the position of Bethel. However, this phrase implies that Amos spoke in many locations in the north, not just Bethel.

The VERB "endure" (BDB 465, KB 463, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used of enduring YHWH's wrath (cf. Joel 2:11; Jer. 10:10). The Israelites were listening to Amos!

entries.title: Amos 7:10-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:10-17 This prose account of an encounter between YHWH's spokesman and the leader of the Bethel sanctuary breaks into the context of several judgment visions (poetry):

  1. locusts, Amos 7:1-3
  2. fire or famine, 7:4-6 (cf. Amos 8:11-13)
  3. plumb line, Amos 7:7-9
  4. summer fruit, Amos 8:1-3
  5. earthquake, Amos 9:1-2 (possibly Amos 8:7-10)

entries.title: Amos 7:11 "For thus Amos says, ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword'"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:11 "For thus Amos says, ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword'" This refers to Jeroboam II. Amaziah slightly misquoted Amos, but in reality it was the essence of his message.

▣ "Israel will certainly go from its land into exile" This was a staggering judgment pronouncement. The Promised Land is no longer under YHWH's protection! No, quite the opposite; it is under YHWH's attack. Israel had allowed the confiscation of the land allotments (by the wealthy, powerful, and influential) of her farmers and now YHWH revoked His covenant promise!

The Exile of Israel by Assyria is mentioned several times by Amos (cf. Amos 4:2-3; 5:5,27; 6:7; 7:17; 9:4,14).

entries.title: Amos 7:12 "Go. . .flee away"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:12 "Go. . .flee away" These are both Qal IMPERATIVES ("go" BDB 229, KB 246, "flee" BDB 137, KB 156). There is a third Qal IMPERATIVE later in the verse, "eat" (BDB 37, KB 46). Amaziah wants Amos to get out of the sanctuary, the city, and the country!

▣ "you seer" Amaziah called Amos a seer possibly because of his public proclamation of his visions. It was a synonym for "prophet."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DIFFERENT HEBREW TERMS FOR PROPHET

▣ "flee away to the land of Judah" Possibly Amaziah was charging Amos with being prejudiced against Israel or a meddling foreigner (i.e. from Judah, see Introduction to Amos, IV).

▣ "there eat bread and there do your prophesying" Apparently, some prophets were supported by the state, while others lived on the freewill offerings of the people to whom they preached. Amaziah was accusing Amos of preaching for money. Amos seems to answer in Amos 7:14 that he already had a source of income.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

entries.title: Amos 7:13 "for it is a sanctuary of the king and a royal residence"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:13 "for it is a sanctuary of the king and a royal residence" It is obvious that Amaziah was expressing the truth ironically when he states this is not God's sanctuary but the king's. The reference here is, of course, to one of the national shrines set up by Jeroboam I that became the site of the official state religion of the Northern Ten Tribes. It was later corrupted by Ahab and Jezebel (cf. 1 Kgs. 18-21) into the worship of the fertility gods of Canaan (i.e. Ba'al, Astarte).

entries.title: Amos 7:14 "I am not a prophet, nor am I the son of a prophet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:14 "I am not a prophet, nor am I the son of a prophet" Amos was asserting YHWH's call to speak not to a profession (cf. Amos 7:15), a VERB must be supplied in this statement. The PRESENT TENSE fits this context, but not Amos 7:15. It could be translated, "I was not a prophet." Implication, but now I am.

This statement by Amos seems to contrast "prophet" with "son of a prophet." If so, the distinction would be between a person called to speak for God as an individual versus a person called by God to be a part of a group of prophets (i.e. Samuel, 1 Sam. 10:5,6,10; 19:20; 1 Kgs. 20:35; 2 Kgs. 2:3-7; 4:38; 6:1). In the latter case "son" would refer to a member of a group, not a family.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Sons of. . .

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), I. A. 2. a. (3)

▣ "for I am a herdsman and a grower of sycamore figs" See full notes in Introduction IV. In this context it may function as a way of showing Amos' wealth or occupation. He did not need to prophesy to eat!

The VERB "grower" (BDB 118, KB 134, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE means "to pierce with the finger nail or tool, to cause fruit to rippen."

The "sycamore figs" are the fruit of this common tree in Palestine. Its fruit resembles "figs," but must be hand pierced to ripen. It was a common food source for the poor. See UBS, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 179-182.

entries.title: Amos 7:15 "took me from following the flock"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:15 "took me from following the flock" This VERB (BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT) has a strong theological connotation of YHWH's sovereign choice and action (e.g. Exod. 6:7; Deut. 4:20,34; 2 Sam. 7:8; 1 Kgs. 11:37; Jer. 43:10). God called Amos to speak for Him!

This is a play on the word "shepherd," used as imagery for

  1. God Himself
  2. Israel's leaders
  3. by implication, the nation

Israel and Judah as a whole were YHWH's sheep (i.e. Psalm 23).

▣ "Go prophesy to My people Israel" There are several IMPERATIVES in this context.

  1. "Go," BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  3. "Hear," Amos 7:16, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE

▣ "My people Israel" This is a Covenant phrase (cf. Amos 7:8,15; 8:2) using Jacob's new name (cf. Gen. 32:28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Amos 7:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:16 This is Amos characterizing Amaziah's words, which were opposite of YHWH's.

▣
NASB, NRSV, NET, JPSOA  "do not preach against"
NKJV  "do not spout against"
REB  "speak out against"
NJB  "do not foretell doom"
TEV  "stop raving against"
Peshitta  "do not teach against"
LXX  "raise not a tumult"

The MT has "do not preach" (BDB 642, KB 694, Hiphil IMPERFECT, NEGATED), which comes from a root meaning "to drip" and is parallel to "prophesy" (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERFECT). As Amaziah's comment in several places is negative,

  1. Amos has conspired against you, v. 10
  2. go, you seer, v. 12
  3. flee away to Judah, v. 12
  4. eat bread (in Judah), v. 12
  5. no longer prophesy at Bethel, v. 13
  6. do not prophesy against Israel, v. 16
  7. do not preach (i.e. "drip") against Israel, v. 16

▣ "against the house of Isaac" This is the only use of this phrase in the OT. It may be parallel to

  1. "house of Jacob" (cf. Amos 3:13)
  2. "house of Israel" (cf. Amos 5:1,3,4,25; 6:1)

It was a disparaging comment by Amaziah about Amos' preaching in the north.

entries.title: Amos 7:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:17 Amos says this priest's wife will be publicly raped (and become a common prostitute), his children killed, his property divided among others, and he, himself, will go into exile for life in Assyria. He will be an example of what will happen to all of Israel's leaders.

In a real sense these judgments on Amaziah meant that neither he nor his descendants would be priests.

  1. Wife will be unfit for marriage to a priest (cf. Deut. 22:23-24).
  2. No children will survive him.
  3. He dies in a foreign land unable to pass on his priestly credentials.

(See David A. Hubbard, Joel and Amos (Tyndale Old Testament Commentary, p. 217).

▣ "by a measuring line" The "line" (BDB 286 I, #2) refers to a measuring cord.

  1. for judgment ‒ 2 Sam. 8:2; Micah 2:5
  2. for inheritance ‒ Ps. 16:5; 78:55
  3. for restoration ‒ Zech. 1:16; 2:1

In Revelation, John uses this imagery for the new heaven and earth, Rev. 11:1,2; 21:15-17.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Does God change His mind? How?
  2. How is repentance related to forgiveness?
  3. How do you know who truly speaks for God? (Prophet, Priest, or Sage)
  4. Is God's judgment eschatological or temporal?

entries.title: Amos 8:1 "Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:1 "Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold" This phrase was used to introduce the first three visions in chapter 7. Because of its recurrent use it shows that the visions are related (cf. Amos 7:1,4,7; 8:1).

▣ "a basket of summer fruit" There is a word play in the Hebrew text between the word for "fruit" (קיצ, BDB 884, KB 1098) and the word for "end" (קצ, BDB 893, KB 1118, cf. Dan. 8:17,19; 11:40; 12:4,6) in Amos 8:2. These two words would have been pronounced the same way (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 920).

Summer fruit (BDB 884) is the last fruit of the season, which over ripens very quickly in the heat and was appropriate imagery for the spiritual rottenness of the Israeli nation. They were over-ripe for judgment!

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above.
